# The web stack {#sec-the-web-stack}

Almost every system in this tutorial is reached in the same way. A client resolves a name, opens a connection, secures
it, sends an HTTP request and waits for the response; on the way the request passes a load balancer, perhaps an edge
server of a content delivery network, and an application server that must recognise who sent it. This chapter takes
that path apart. Its claims are again of two kinds. The components and protocols (the request path, load balancers,
content delivery networks, stateless services, the styles of an interface, the methods of real-time delivery, sessions,
tokens and OAuth 2.0) are definitions, written precisely enough that their properties can be checked. The results that
designers rely on when they size and tune these components, such as how many round trips a new request costs, how
unevenly random assignment spreads load, what hit ratio an expiring cache reaches, why cursor-based pagination neither
repeats nor skips items and what polling costs, are propositions with complete proofs. Results whose proofs are long and
belong to probability theory, such as the power of two choices, are stated as quoted from their source.

The sources are the four benchmark books of the tutorial, three section sources, a survey and the standards that define
the protocols. The request path follows @SystemDesignInterview2021 [Ch. 1], @sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024 [Ch. 4],
@liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 5, "Networking"] and @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Sec. 6.7], with the protocol rules from
@rfc9293, @rfc8446, @rfc5246, @rfc9110 and @rfc9112. Load balancing follows @sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024 [Ch. 4] and
@tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Sec. 3.1], with @mitzenmacher2001power for randomised assignment. Content delivery networks
follow @SystemDesignInterview2021 [Ch. 1], @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Sec. 1.4.4 and Ch. 13],
@liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 5] and @reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022 [App. B], with freshness from @rfc9111.
Interfaces follow @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Secs. 6.7 and 12.7.1], @sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024 [Ch. 8],
@liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Chs. 2 and 5], @pachecoPrinciplesSoftwareArchitecture2024 [Ch. 6] and
@gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024 [Chs. 5-6]. Real-time delivery follows @liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 5],
@SystemDesignInterview2021 [Ch. 12] and @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Sec. 6.7.5], with @rfc6202, @rfc6455 and
@whatwgHTML [Sec. 9.2]. Authentication and authorisation follow @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [App. B],
@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024 [Ch. 8], @liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 5 and App. 6] and
@gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024 [Ch. 10], with @rfc6265, @rfc6749, @rfc6750, @rfc7519, @rfc7636, @rfc9700 and
@oidcCore. The probability comes from
[Probability and statistics](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd), and the
estimates, availabilities and latency budgets of [Estimation and the design process](../estimation-and-the-design-process/index.qmd)
are used throughout.

The chapter has seven sections. @sec-request-path defines the request path and counts the round trips of a new request.
@sec-load-balancing defines load balancers and proves how round-robin and random assignment spread requests.
@sec-cdn defines content delivery networks and proves the hit ratio of an expiring cache. @sec-stateless-scaling
defines stateless services and the two ways of scaling. @sec-apis defines the styles and properties of web interfaces
and proves the correctness of keyset pagination. @sec-real-time defines the methods of real-time delivery and proves
their delay and cost. @sec-auth defines sessions and tokens, then the OAuth 2.0 authorisation-code grant and OpenID
Connect.

The running example is the photo-sharing service of the previous chapter (@exm-req-photoshare), with its workload
unchanged (@exm-req-workload-assumptions): $10^8$ daily active users, $50$ feed pages per user and day, a peak factor of
$3$, feed pages of ten $30\,\mathrm{kB}$ thumbnails, and $146$ application servers for the feed at its peak of
$1.74 \times 10^5$ requests per second (@exm-load-servers).

Every definition and proposition is followed by ten examples and ten exercises, each exercise with a hidden solution
in two tabs: the argument, then a computation with its recorded output. The computations run in plain Python 3.12 with
NumPy, the standard library (`http.client`, `sqlite3`, `hashlib`, `hmac`, `urllib`) and, for simulations, SimPy 4.1.2.
Diagrams are written in the D2 language, and an exercise that asks for a diagram shows its source next to the drawing.
Configurations and command-line sessions that would need a running server are marked as illustrative and are not run.

## The request path {#sec-request-path}

Xu begins his book with a single server and the four steps that bring a request to it: the client looks up a domain
name, receives an IP address, sends an HTTP request to that address and receives HTML or JSON in return
[@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 1, "Single server setup"]. Each step is a protocol of its own, run by different
machines, and each costs time before the application does any work. Liu warns that a designer who cannot say what
happens between the browser and the server "trivializes the complexity of routing requests through the internet"
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Networking"]. This section defines the path of one request, layer by layer, with
the rules of the standards that define each protocol, and then proves how many round trips a new request costs before
its first byte of response arrives. Every later component of the chapter sits somewhere on this path.

For more on this topic, see @SystemDesignInterview2021 [Ch. 1], @sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024 [Ch. 4, "Exploring DNS"],
@liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 5, "Networking"] and @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Secs. 1.4.1-1.4.2 and 6.7.1].

### Layers and the path of one request

The Internet's protocols are layered: "the protocols of each level are implemented using protocols of the lower level"
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 6.7.1]. A designer needs four of them for an ordinary web request, one for each thing
that must happen before an application server sees the request: a name must become an address, a reliable byte stream
must be set up to that address, the stream must be made confidential and authenticated, and the request and response
must be framed as messages. The definition lists them in that order and records, for each, the rule that decides when
the next message may be sent, because those rules decide the latency.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-request-path}
#### Request path

Let a client send a request to a service named by a host name $H$ in an `https` URI. Its **request path** is the
sequence of four protocol exchanges below, each running over the one after it in the list of layers (application:
DNS and HTTP; security: TLS; transport: TCP; network: IP).

1. **Name resolution** (DNS). The client asks a **resolver** for the address records of $H$. The resolver answers from
   its cache or by querying the hierarchy of name servers (root, top-level domain, authoritative). Every record carries
   a **time to live** (TTL): "the time interval that the resource record may be cached before the source of the
   information should again be consulted" [@rfc1035, Sec. 3.2.1].
2. **Transport connection** (TCP). The client opens a connection to the address and port $443$, the default for
   `https` [@rfc9110, Sec. 4.2.2], by the three-way handshake: SYN from the client, SYN-ACK from the server, ACK from the
   client. The client may send data with or after its ACK, and the server delivers data to the layer above only once the
   connection is established [@rfc9293, Sec. 3.5].
3. **Secure channel** (TLS). Client and server run the TLS handshake over the connection, which authenticates the server
   and establishes keys. In the full TLS 1.3 handshake the client sends a ClientHello, the server answers with one flight
   ending in its Finished message, and the client sends its own Finished, after which application data flows in both
   directions [@rfc8446, Sec. 2].
4. **HTTP exchange**. The client sends a **request message** (a request line with method, target and version, header
   fields, an empty line, an optional body) and the server answers with a **response message** (a status line, header
   fields, an empty line, an optional body) [@rfc9112, Sec. 2.1]. An HTTP/1.1 connection is **persistent** by default:
   it carries further requests until one side closes it [@rfc9112, Sec. 9.3].

The **round-trip time** $\mathrm{RTT}$ between two machines is the time from sending a short message to receiving the
immediate reply, without processing. An **intermediary** is a machine on the path that terminates the client's
connection and opens its own to the next machine, such as a proxy; the path then consists of one sequence of steps 2 to
4 per connection.
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Xu's four steps are the coarsest description of the path. Matching them with the definition shows what they leave
out.

::: {#exm-net-xu-request-flow}
#### Xu's request flow

Xu's steps are: users access the site "through domain names, such as api.mysite.com"; the IP address "is returned to
the browser or mobile app"; then "HTTP requests are sent directly to your web server", which "returns HTML pages or JSON
response" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 1, "Single server setup"]. His first two steps are item 1 of the definition
and his last two are item 4. Items 2 and 3, the TCP and TLS handshakes, are not mentioned, although on a new connection
each of them costs a round trip of its own before the request can be sent.
:::

Name resolution is itself a distributed system. Sinha and Chopra describe its hierarchy of servers and the role of the
resolver that walks it.

::: {#exm-net-dns-hierarchy}
#### The DNS hierarchy

"Root servers point to TLD servers, which point to authoritative servers that finally resolve domain names to IP
addresses" [@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 4, "Exploring DNS"]. To resolve `photos.example.com` with an empty cache,
a resolver asks a root server (which refers it to the servers of `com`), a `com` server (which refers it to the
authoritative servers of `example.com`) and an authoritative server (which returns the address). Every answer is cached
by the resolver for its TTL, so the next client of the same resolver gets the address without any of these queries.
:::

The TTL is what makes the hierarchy scale, and it is also what makes changes slow. Sinha and Chopra name both effects.

::: {#exm-net-dns-ttl}
#### What the TTL buys and costs

DNS "achieves high performance by sacrificing strong consistency", providing "eventual consistency through techniques
such as time-to-live for cached records", and an update can take "from seconds to days" to reach every server
[@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 4, "Consistency"]. With a TTL of $300\,\mathrm{s}$, a resolver that cached the old
address just before a change keeps returning it for up to five minutes; with a TTL of a day, for up to a day. Liu adds
that the browser caches the answer too, and "the server has no control over the client-side browser cache"
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "How to Route to the Closest Region"].
:::

A name server may answer different clients differently. Tan uses this to send each user to the nearest data centre.

::: {#exm-net-geodns}
#### GeoDNS

When a client resolves Tan's `beigel.com`, "GeoDNS obtains the client's location from their IP address and assigns the
client the corresponding host IP address", so that clients in North America, Asia and Europe reach the data centres in
the United States, Singapore and Amsterdam; it is done "by assigning multiple A records to our domain for various
locations and a default IP address for other locations" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 1.4.2, pp. 7-8]. Item 1 of the
definition is unchanged; only the resolver's answer depends on who asks.
:::

The other way to reach a nearby machine works one layer lower, in the routing of IP packets. Liu calls it the edge
router option.

::: {#exm-net-anycast}
#### Anycast

"In an anycast, multiple edges can be assigned the same IP"; each router forwards a packet towards the nearest of them,
and the edge router forwards the request to "the most optimal data center"
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "How to Route to the Closest Region", Option 2]. Here DNS returns the same address
to everyone, and the network layer, below TCP, chooses the machine. Liu notes the advantage over DNS: clients that
cache an address do not keep sending to a failed server, since the address itself moves.
:::

The layers of the definition are a selection from the seven-layer reference model. Tan's table places each protocol in
it.

::: {#exm-net-osi}
#### Layers of the reference model

Tan's table of the OSI model puts HTTP in layer 7 (application), TCP and UDP in layer 4 (transport), IP in layer 3
(network), Ethernet and Wi-Fi in layer 2, and puts encryption in layer 6 (presentation)
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 6.7.1, Table 6.2, p. 138]. TLS runs between HTTP and TCP, which is why the definition
lists it as a layer of its own. Liu's advice is to know "which layer" a term belongs to, since "TCP and HTTP are ...
different things and solve different problems" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "OSI Model"]; for a generalist,
he adds, "layer 7 and layer 4 are the most important ones to be familiar with".
:::

The three-way handshake is the first exchange of item 2. The standard's own trace shows its three segments and the data
that may follow the third.

::: {#exm-net-tcp-handshake}
#### The three-way handshake

In the basic trace of RFC 9293, peer A sends `<SEQ=100><CTL=SYN>`, peer B answers `<SEQ=300><ACK=101><CTL=SYN,ACK>`,
and A sends `<SEQ=101><ACK=301><CTL=ACK>`, after which "TCP Peer A sends some data" with the same sequence number 101
[@rfc9293, Sec. 3.5, Figure 6]. The standard allows data on the earlier segments too, but the receiver buffers it "until
the connection reaches the ESTABLISHED state", which happens at B when the ACK arrives. Either way B's application sees
the first byte one and a half round trips after A started.
:::

The TLS 1.3 handshake of item 3 has three phases. Only the first message of each side carries no encryption.

::: {#exm-net-tls13}
#### The TLS 1.3 handshake

The ClientHello carries the client's key shares and offered algorithms; the server's ServerHello carries its key share,
after which "everything after this phase is encrypted"; the server then sends its parameters, its certificate, a
signature over the handshake (CertificateVerify) and Finished; the client checks them and sends its Finished
[@rfc8446, Sec. 2, Figure 1]. Application data from the client can travel with its Finished. Compared with TLS 1.2, in
which the client's key exchange comes only after the server's first flight [@rfc5246, Sec. 7.3, Figure 1], one round trip
is saved.
:::

The messages of item 4 are text in HTTP/1.1. A request for the first feed page of the running example and its response
look like this.

::: {#exm-net-http-message}
#### A feed request and its response

The request is `GET /feed?page=1 HTTP/1.1`, then the header fields `Host: photos.example.com`, `Accept:
application/json` and `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, then an empty line. The response is `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`, then
`Content-Type: application/json`, `Content-Length: 2154` and `Cache-Control: private, max-age=0`, an empty line and
$2154$ bytes of JSON listing ten photos with the URLs of their thumbnails. The thumbnails themselves are fetched by
further requests, which on a persistent connection [@rfc9112, Sec. 9.3] reuse the connection already set up.
:::

The whole path can be watched with a command-line client. The session below is illustrative: it needs the network and a
real server, and its timings would differ on every run.

::: {#exm-net-curl-session}
#### Watching the path with curl

The verbose mode of `curl` prints the steps of the definition as they happen, and its `-w` option prints the time at
which each one ended.

```{.code .illustrative}
# Illustrative: needs network access and a server; not run, no recorded output.
$ curl -sv -o /dev/null https://photos.example.com/feed?page=1 \
    -w 'dns %{time_namelookup}  tcp %{time_connect}  tls %{time_appconnect}  first byte %{time_starttransfer}\n'
*   Trying 203.0.113.10:443...                 # item 1 done: the resolver returned 203.0.113.10
* Connected to photos.example.com port 443     # item 2: the three-way handshake
* SSL connection using TLSv1.3                 # item 3: the TLS handshake
> GET /feed?page=1 HTTP/1.1                    # item 4: the request message
> Host: photos.example.com
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK                              # the status line of the response
< Content-Type: application/json
dns 0.012  tcp 0.052  tls 0.093  first byte 0.161
```

Each printed time is cumulative from the start, so the differences are the durations of the steps.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise is the computation the coverage of this section asks for: parsing a request and a response with the
standard library, as a server and a client do.

::: {#exr-net-parse-http}
#### Parsing a request and a response

Using only the standard library, parse the request and the response of @exm-net-http-message from their bytes: give the
method, target and version of the request and its `Host` field, then the status code, the `Content-Type` and the body
of the response. What tells the parser where the header section ends?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The start line is everything up to the first CRLF; for a request it splits at spaces into method, target and version.
The header section ends at the empty line, the first occurrence of two consecutive CRLFs [@rfc9112, Sec. 2.1]. The body
of the response has the length given by `Content-Length`. The standard library's `http.client` parses the header fields
of either message and the whole response.

## Python

The request is split by hand and its fields parsed by `http.client.parse_headers`; the response is read by
`http.client.HTTPResponse` from an in-memory socket.

```{.python .run}
import http.client, io, json
request = (b"GET /feed?page=1 HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: photos.example.com\r\n"
           b"Accept: application/json\r\nAuthorization: Bearer abc\r\n\r\n")
start, rest = request.split(b"\r\n", 1)
method, target, version = start.decode().split(" ")
fields = http.client.parse_headers(io.BytesIO(rest))
print(method, target, version, "| Host:", fields["Host"])

body = json.dumps({"page": 1, "photos": [{"id": i} for i in range(3)]}).encode()
response = (b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: application/json\r\n"
            b"Content-Length: " + str(len(body)).encode() + b"\r\nCache-Control: private, max-age=0\r\n\r\n" + body)

class Socket:                      # http.client reads the response from sock.makefile("rb")
    def __init__(self, data): self.data = data
    def makefile(self, mode): return io.BytesIO(self.data)

r = http.client.HTTPResponse(Socket(response))
r.begin()
print(r.status, r.reason, "|", r.getheader("Content-Type"), "|", json.loads(r.read()))
print("end of header section at byte", response.index(b"\r\n\r\n") + 4, "of", len(response))
```

```{.text .run-output}
GET /feed?page=1 HTTP/1.1 | Host: photos.example.com
200 OK | application/json | {'page': 1, 'photos': [{'id': 0}, {'id': 1}, {'id': 2}]}
end of header section at byte 106 of 162
```
::::
:::

The second exercise places the protocols of a request in their layers. It uses Tan's table of the reference model.

::: {#exr-net-layers}
#### Which layer?

Assign each of DNS, HTTP, TLS, TCP, UDP, IP and Ethernet to a layer of Tan's table (@exm-net-osi), and say over which
transport DNS queries usually travel, using Sinha and Chopra's remark that DNS "uses the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) for
most queries and responses" [@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 4, "Reliability"]. Why does that make a DNS lookup cost
one round trip, without a handshake?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

DNS and HTTP are application protocols (layer 7); TLS provides the encryption Tan places in layer 6; TCP and UDP are
layer 4; IP is layer 3; Ethernet is layer 2. A DNS query is a single UDP datagram and the answer another, with no
connection to set up, so an uncached lookup to a resolver costs one round trip plus the resolver's own work; a lost
datagram is handled by resending it, as Sinha and Chopra say.

## Python

The assignment as a table, sorted from the top layer down.

```{.python .run}
layer = {"DNS": 7, "HTTP": 7, "TLS": 6, "TCP": 4, "UDP": 4, "IP": 3, "Ethernet": 2}
name = {7: "application", 6: "presentation", 4: "transport", 3: "network", 2: "data link"}
for protocol, k in sorted(layer.items(), key=lambda item: -item[1]):
    print(f"{protocol:8s} layer {k} ({name[k]})")
print("handshakes before a DNS answer over UDP:", 0)
```

```{.text .run-output}
DNS      layer 7 (application)
HTTP     layer 7 (application)
TLS      layer 6 (presentation)
TCP      layer 4 (transport)
UDP      layer 4 (transport)
IP       layer 3 (network)
Ethernet layer 2 (data link)
handshakes before a DNS answer over UDP: 0
```
::::
:::

The third exercise checks a number in one of the benchmark books against the standard. It is the default port of the
`http` scheme.

::: {#exr-net-default-port}
#### The default port of http

Liu writes that HTTPS uses "the default port 443" and that "HTTP's (without the s for secure) default port is 8080"
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "IP and Port"]. Check both against RFC 9110 and against the constants of Python's
`http.client`. What happens to a client that follows Liu's second statement?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The first is right: "TCP port 443 (the reserved port for HTTP over TLS) is the default" [@rfc9110, Sec. 4.2.2]. The
second is wrong: for an `http` URI without a port, "TCP port 80 (the reserved port for WWW services) is the default"
[@rfc9110, Sec. 4.2.1]; $8080$ is only a common choice for test servers. A client that connected to port $8080$ for
`http://photos.example.com/` would reach nothing, or a different service.

## Python

The library's constants and the port that `urllib.parse` reports for URIs with and without an explicit port.

```{.python .run}
import http.client
from urllib.parse import urlsplit
print("http.client.HTTP_PORT =", http.client.HTTP_PORT, "| HTTPS_PORT =", http.client.HTTPS_PORT)
for uri in ("http://photos.example.com/", "http://photos.example.com:8080/", "https://photos.example.com/"):
    u = urlsplit(uri)
    port = u.port or {"http": http.client.HTTP_PORT, "https": http.client.HTTPS_PORT}[u.scheme]
    print(f"{uri:34s} -> port {port}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
http.client.HTTP_PORT = 80 | HTTPS_PORT = 443
http://photos.example.com/         -> port 80
http://photos.example.com:8080/    -> port 8080
https://photos.example.com/        -> port 443
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise makes the cost of a long TTL concrete. It asks how long clients keep using an address after the
record has been changed.

::: {#exr-net-dns-failover}
#### Failing over through DNS

A service changes its address record at time $0$, after its old data centre failed. The record's TTL is $\Delta$, and
the resolvers of its clients last refreshed the record at times spread uniformly over $(-\Delta, 0]$. What fraction of
resolvers still returns the old address at time $t \in [0, \Delta]$? How long until all have the new one, for $\Delta =
60\,\mathrm{s}$ and $\Delta = 3600\,\mathrm{s}$, and why does Sinha and Chopra's remark that "recovery through DNS can be
slow due to caching" [@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 4, "DNS and GSLB"] hold even after that?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A resolver that refreshed at time $-u$ keeps the old address until $\Delta - u$. With $u$ uniform on $[0, \Delta)$ the
old address is still returned at time $t$ when $\Delta - u > t$, that is $u < \Delta - t$, with probability $1 -
t/\Delta$. All resolvers have the new address after $\Delta$: one minute or one hour. Browsers and operating systems
cache the answer again for up to the same TTL, and some clients cache longer than they should, which the service cannot
control; the worst case is therefore longer than $\Delta$.

## Python

The fraction of stale resolvers at a few times, from the formula and from $10^5$ seeded refresh times.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
for ttl in (60, 3600):
    u = rng.uniform(0, ttl, 100_000)
    for t in (0, ttl / 4, ttl / 2, ttl):
        print(f"TTL {ttl:4d} s, t = {t:6.0f} s: stale {1 - t / ttl:.3f} (simulated {np.mean(ttl - u > t):.3f})")
```

```{.text .run-output}
TTL   60 s, t =      0 s: stale 1.000 (simulated 1.000)
TTL   60 s, t =     15 s: stale 0.750 (simulated 0.749)
TTL   60 s, t =     30 s: stale 0.500 (simulated 0.500)
TTL   60 s, t =     60 s: stale 0.000 (simulated 0.000)
TTL 3600 s, t =      0 s: stale 1.000 (simulated 1.000)
TTL 3600 s, t =    900 s: stale 0.750 (simulated 0.750)
TTL 3600 s, t =   1800 s: stale 0.500 (simulated 0.501)
TTL 3600 s, t =   3600 s: stale 0.000 (simulated 0.000)
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise shows why a resolver's cache protects the name servers. It counts the queries that reach the
authoritative servers.

::: {#exr-net-dns-load}
#### Load on the authoritative servers

The photo service's name is resolved by $10^4$ resolvers, each serving many clients, and the record's TTL is $\Delta =
300\,\mathrm{s}$. A resolver queries the authoritative servers only when its cached record has expired and a client asks.
Show that the authoritative servers receive at most $10^4/\Delta$ queries per second for this record however many
clients there are, and compare with the $1.74 \times 10^5$ feed requests per second at peak.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

After a query at time $t$ a resolver holds the record until $t + \Delta$ and sends no further query before then. Its
queries are therefore at least $\Delta$ apart, and in any interval of length $T$ it sends at most $T/\Delta + 1$. Summed
over the resolvers, the rate is at most $10^4/300 = 33.3$ queries per second in the long run, whatever the number of
clients. Even if every feed request were preceded by a lookup, the name servers would see five thousand times fewer
queries than the application.

## Python

The bound, and a seeded check: $10^4$ resolvers, each receiving client requests at a random rate, over one hour.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
ttl, hour, resolvers = 300, 3600, 10_000
queries = 0
for rate in rng.uniform(0.001, 5, resolvers):           # client requests per second at this resolver
    times = np.cumsum(rng.exponential(1 / rate, int(rate * hour * 1.2) + 10))
    times = times[times < hour]
    expires = -1.0
    for t in times:
        if t >= expires:
            queries, expires = queries + 1, t + ttl
print(f"bound {resolvers / ttl:.1f} per second; simulated {queries / hour:.1f} per second")
print(f"feed requests per authoritative query at the bound: {1.74e5 / (resolvers / ttl):,.0f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
bound 33.3 per second; simulated 33.3 per second
feed requests per authoritative query at the bound: 5,220
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise checks a claim about HTTP against the standard. It is Tan's description of HTTP connections.

::: {#exr-net-persistent}
#### Does HTTP open a connection per request?

Tan contrasts WebSocket with "HTTP, which creates a new connection for every request and closes it with every response"
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 6.7.5, p. 142]. Check this against RFC 9112, and compute the handshakes saved when a
client fetches the feed page and its ten thumbnails over one connection instead of eleven, with $\mathrm{RTT} =
80\,\mathrm{ms}$ and a TCP and a TLS 1.3 handshake of one round trip each (@def-request-path).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The claim describes HTTP/1.0 without keep-alive. "HTTP/1.1 defaults to the use of 'persistent connections', allowing
multiple requests and responses to be carried over a single connection" [@rfc9112, Sec. 9.3]; a connection closes after
a response only if one side sends the `close` option. Reusing one connection for eleven requests saves ten TCP and ten
TLS handshakes, $20$ round trips, $1.6\,\mathrm{s}$ if the requests are sent one after another.

## Python

The round trips with and without reuse, for requests sent one after another.

```{.python .run}
rtt, requests, handshake = 0.080, 11, 2                  # TCP + TLS 1.3: one round trip each
fresh = requests * (handshake + 1) * rtt
reused = (handshake + requests) * rtt
print(f"new connection per request: {fresh:.2f} s; one persistent connection: {reused:.2f} s; saved {fresh - reused:.2f} s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
new connection per request: 2.64 s; one persistent connection: 1.04 s; saved 1.60 s
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise turns the handshake rule of item 2 into a small program. It follows the states of the standard's
trace.

::: {#exr-net-handshake-states}
#### The handshake as a state machine

Write the client and server sides of the basic three-way handshake as state machines with the states CLOSED, LISTEN,
SYN-SENT, SYN-RECEIVED and ESTABLISHED [@rfc9293, Sec. 3.5, Figure 6], exchange the three segments, and print each
side's state after each segment. When may each side first hand data to its application?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The client goes CLOSED, SYN-SENT (after sending SYN), ESTABLISHED (on receiving SYN-ACK); the server goes LISTEN,
SYN-RECEIVED (on receiving SYN), ESTABLISHED (on receiving ACK). The client may send data on its ACK; the server hands
data to its application only in ESTABLISHED, that is on receiving the ACK, one and a half round trips after the client
started.

## Python

The two machines and the trace, with the times of arrival in round trips.

```{.python .run}
client, server = {"state": "CLOSED"}, {"state": "LISTEN"}
def step(t, segment, sender, receiver, sender_state, receiver_state):
    sender["state"], receiver["state"] = sender_state or sender["state"], receiver_state
    print(f"t = {t:.1f} RTT  {segment:8s} client {client['state']:12s} server {server['state']}")
client["state"] = "SYN-SENT"
step(0.5, "SYN", client, server, None, "SYN-RECEIVED")
step(1.0, "SYN-ACK", server, client, None, "ESTABLISHED")
step(1.5, "ACK", client, server, None, "ESTABLISHED")
```

```{.text .run-output}
t = 0.5 RTT  SYN      client SYN-SENT     server SYN-RECEIVED
t = 1.0 RTT  SYN-ACK  client ESTABLISHED  server SYN-RECEIVED
t = 1.5 RTT  ACK      client ESTABLISHED  server ESTABLISHED
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise compares the headers of a small request with its payload. It explains why the framing of messages
matters for frequent small requests.

::: {#exr-net-header-overhead}
#### Header overhead

An API call sends a JSON body of $40$ bytes in a POST request with the request line and the fields `Host`,
`Content-Type`, `Content-Length`, `Authorization` (a credential of $800$ bytes) and `User-Agent`, and receives a
$20$-byte body with a status line and three fields. Compute the bytes of each message and the fraction that is payload.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Counting every byte, including the CRLFs, the request is about $1010$ bytes, of which $40$ are payload, about $4\%$;
the response is about $130$ bytes with $20$ of payload, $15\%$. The credential alone outweighs the body twentyfold. For frequent
small requests the framing, not the data, decides the bandwidth.

## Python

The two messages built byte by byte.

```{.python .run}
token = "t" * 800
body = b'{"photo": 123456, "action": "like-it"}  '
req = (f"POST /photos/123456/likes HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: photos.example.com\r\nContent-Type: application/json\r\n"
       f"Content-Length: {len(body)}\r\nAuthorization: Bearer {token}\r\nUser-Agent: photoshare-ios/5.2\r\n\r\n").encode() + body
rbody = b'{"likes": 1024}     '
resp = (f"HTTP/1.1 201 Created\r\nContent-Type: application/json\r\nContent-Length: {len(rbody)}\r\n"
        f"Location: /photos/123456/likes/9\r\n\r\n").encode() + rbody
for name, msg, payload in (("request", req, body), ("response", resp, rbody)):
    print(f"{name:8s}: {len(msg)} bytes, payload {len(payload)} ({len(payload) / len(msg):.1%})")
```

```{.text .run-output}
request : 1012 bytes, payload 40 (4.0%)
response: 130 bytes, payload 20 (15.4%)
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise counts the queries of a resolution with and without a caching resolver. It tests a claim of Sinha
and Chopra about recursion.

::: {#exr-net-recursive-load}
#### Recursive resolution and the load on the root

Sinha and Chopra ask which of iterative and recursive queries reduces the load on the DNS infrastructure and answer
"it is not recursive", because recursion "will require an increase in memory to maintain the recursion structure"
[@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 4, "DNS querying"]. Consider $10^6$ clients that each resolve `photos.example.com`
once an hour, with a TTL of one hour for every record. Count the queries per hour that reach the root, `com` and
authoritative servers (a) if every client walks the hierarchy itself without a cache, and (b) if the clients use $10^3$
shared caching resolvers that walk it for them. What actually reduces the load?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

(a) Each client sends one query to each level per hour: $10^6$ queries per hour to each of the three levels. (b) Each
resolver walks the hierarchy at most once per TTL: at most $10^3$ queries per hour to each level, a thousand times fewer.
What reduces the load is the shared cache of the resolver, not the direction of the query: the resolver is the party
that holds state, and it is the recursive service the clients use. Sinha and Chopra's own section on caching says the
same thing.

## Python

The two counts per level.

```{.python .run}
clients, resolvers, per_hour = 10**6, 10**3, 1
for level in ("root", "com", "authoritative"):
    print(f"{level:13s}: no shared cache {clients * per_hour:>9,}  shared resolvers {resolvers * per_hour:>6,} per hour")
```

```{.text .run-output}
root         : no shared cache 1,000,000  shared resolvers  1,000 per hour
com          : no shared cache 1,000,000  shared resolvers  1,000 per hour
authoritative: no shared cache 1,000,000  shared resolvers  1,000 per hour
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise reads the timings of an illustrative session. It recovers the round-trip time and the server's time
from them.

::: {#exr-net-read-timings}
#### Reading the timings

In @exm-net-curl-session the cumulative times were $12\,\mathrm{ms}$ for the name, $52\,\mathrm{ms}$ for the TCP
connection, $93\,\mathrm{ms}$ for the TLS handshake and $161\,\mathrm{ms}$ for the first byte. Estimate the round-trip
time to the server and the time the server took to produce its response, using one round trip for each of TCP, TLS 1.3
and the request.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The TCP handshake took $52 - 12 = 40\,\mathrm{ms}$ and the TLS handshake $93 - 52 = 41\,\mathrm{ms}$, both one round
trip, so $\mathrm{RTT} \approx 40\,\mathrm{ms}$. From the end of the handshake to the first byte took $161 - 93 =
68\,\mathrm{ms}$: one round trip and the server's time, which is therefore about $28\,\mathrm{ms}$.

## Python

The differences of the cumulative times.

```{.python .run}
t = {"dns": 12, "tcp": 52, "tls": 93, "first byte": 161}
tcp, tls, request = t["tcp"] - t["dns"], t["tls"] - t["tcp"], t["first byte"] - t["tls"]
rtt = (tcp + tls) / 2
print(f"TCP {tcp} ms, TLS {tls} ms, so RTT ~ {rtt:.1f} ms; server time ~ {request - rtt:.1f} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
TCP 40 ms, TLS 41 ms, so RTT ~ 40.5 ms; server time ~ 27.5 ms
```
::::
:::
::::

### Round trips before the first byte

A designer who sets a latency budget for a request (@prp-latency-budget) must know how much of it the protocols consume
before the application starts. The handshakes of @def-request-path are sequential: each message may be sent only after
another has arrived. Counting the longest chain of such dependencies gives the time to the first byte of the response
exactly, under a simple model of the network. The proposition does that for a new connection with TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2,
for a reused connection and for an uncached name.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-net-round-trips}
#### Round trips of a request

Let a client and a server exchange messages with round-trip time $\mathrm{RTT}$: every message takes $\mathrm{RTT}/2$
in either direction and none is lost, processing takes no time except at the server, which sends the first byte of its
response $t_{\mathrm{srv}}$ after the complete request has arrived. Let the endpoints follow the rules of
@def-request-path: the server's TCP delivers data to TLS only once it has received the client's ACK; in TLS 1.3 the
server sends its flight on receiving the ClientHello and the client sends its Finished and its request on receiving the
server's Finished [@rfc8446, Sec. 2]; in TLS 1.2 the client sends its key exchange and Finished on receiving the
server's first flight, the server sends its Finished on receiving the client's, and the client sends its request on
receiving it [@rfc5246, Sec. 7.3]. Let $T$ be the time from the client's first message to the arrival of the first byte
of the response. Then:

(a) on a new TCP connection with a full TLS 1.3 handshake, $T \geq 3\,\mathrm{RTT} + t_{\mathrm{srv}}$;

(b) on a new TCP connection with a full TLS 1.2 handshake, $T \geq 4\,\mathrm{RTT} + t_{\mathrm{srv}}$;

(c) on an established persistent connection, $T \geq \mathrm{RTT} + t_{\mathrm{srv}}$;

(d) if the name must first be resolved by a resolver at round-trip time $\mathrm{RTT}_D$ that answers $t_D$ after the
query arrives, $\mathrm{RTT}_D + t_D$ is added to each bound;

and in each case equality holds when every message is sent as soon as the rules allow.
:::

::::

*Proof.* Call a message *triggered* by another if the rules allow it to be sent only after that one has arrived. If $m'$
is triggered by $m$, then $m'$ is sent no earlier than $m$ arrives, so it arrives at least $\mathrm{RTT}/2$ later than
$m$ arrives; if moreover $m'$ is sent as soon as $m$ arrives, it arrives exactly $\mathrm{RTT}/2$ later. Along a chain of
triggered messages that alternate in direction, the arrival times therefore grow by at least $\mathrm{RTT}/2$ per
message, with equality for immediate sending; the response adds $t_{\mathrm{srv}}$ at the server.

(a) Start at time $0$ with the SYN. The SYN-ACK is triggered by the SYN and arrives at the client at time
$\geq\mathrm{RTT}$. The ClientHello may travel with the ACK or earlier, but the server's TLS receives it only when the ACK
has arrived, and the ACK is triggered by the SYN-ACK: the ClientHello is available to the server at time $\geq
\tfrac32\mathrm{RTT}$. The server's flight, ending in Finished, is triggered by it and arrives at the client at $\geq
2\,\mathrm{RTT}$. The request is triggered by the server's Finished and arrives at $\geq \tfrac52\mathrm{RTT}$. The first
byte of the response is sent $t_{\mathrm{srv}}$ later and arrives at $\geq 3\,\mathrm{RTT} + t_{\mathrm{srv}}$. Every
inequality is an equality when each message is sent at the moment its trigger arrives.

(b) Up to the server's first flight the chain is that of (a): it arrives at the client at $\geq 2\,\mathrm{RTT}$. The
client's key exchange and Finished are triggered by it and arrive at $\geq \tfrac52\mathrm{RTT}$, the server's Finished
is triggered by them and arrives at $\geq 3\,\mathrm{RTT}$, the request arrives at $\geq \tfrac72\mathrm{RTT}$, and the
first byte of the response at $\geq 4\,\mathrm{RTT} + t_{\mathrm{srv}}$, with equality as before.

(c) On an established connection the request can be sent at time $0$; it arrives at $\mathrm{RTT}/2$, and the first byte
of the response at $\mathrm{RTT} + t_{\mathrm{srv}}$, which no schedule can beat.

(d) The SYN is addressed to the server's address, which the client knows only from the resolver's answer. The query
arrives at the resolver at $\mathrm{RTT}_D/2$ and the answer at the client at $\mathrm{RTT}_D + t_D$; from then on the
chains of (a) to (c) apply, shifted by that time. $\square$

The proposition is a lower bound for every real network, since losses and processing only add time, and it is exact in
the idealised one. Two refinements of the standards shorten the chain and are outside its hypotheses: TLS 1.3 can send
"0-RTT" data with the ClientHello when the client resumes an earlier session, "at the cost of certain security
properties" [@rfc8446, Sec. 1.2 and Sec. 2.3], and the first byte is not the whole response, whose transfer adds its
size divided by the bandwidth.

@fig-net-request-sequence draws the chain of part (a) with an uncached name, as in part (d).

![The messages of a new HTTPS request: name resolution, the TCP handshake, the TLS 1.3 handshake and the HTTP
exchange.](figures/request_sequence.svg){#fig-net-request-sequence width=80%}

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Inside one data centre the round trips cost little. Liu's table gives the number.

::: {#exm-rtt-same-dc}
#### Within a data centre

With Liu's round trip of $0.5\,\mathrm{ms}$ within a data centre [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, App. 3], a new TLS 1.3
connection between two services costs $1.5\,\mathrm{ms} + t_{\mathrm{srv}}$ by part (a) and a reused one
$0.5\,\mathrm{ms} + t_{\mathrm{srv}}$ by part (c). For an internal call with $t_{\mathrm{srv}} = 2\,\mathrm{ms}$, a
new connection makes it $1.4$ times slower; this is why services keep pools of open connections to each other.
:::

Across an ocean the same count dominates everything else. The previous chapter used Liu's $150\,\mathrm{ms}$ between
California and the Netherlands.

::: {#exm-rtt-atlantic}
#### Across the Atlantic

With $\mathrm{RTT} = 150\,\mathrm{ms}$, part (a) gives $450\,\mathrm{ms} + t_{\mathrm{srv}}$ for a new connection and
part (b) $600\,\mathrm{ms} + t_{\mathrm{srv}}$ with TLS 1.2. @exm-budget-ocean counted two round trips, one for the
connection and one for the request; with TLS there are three. No server, however fast, answers a new client in
California from the Netherlands in less than half a second.
:::

Part (c) is what persistent connections buy. Its saving is the same for every request after the first.

::: {#exm-rtt-reuse}
#### What reuse saves

Each request after the first on a persistent connection saves $2\,\mathrm{RTT}$ with TLS 1.3 and $3\,\mathrm{RTT}$ with
TLS 1.2, compared with a new connection. For the feed page and its ten thumbnails over a path with $\mathrm{RTT} =
80\,\mathrm{ms}$, sent one after another, this is the $1.6\,\mathrm{s}$ of @exr-net-persistent.
:::

Part (d) adds the lookup. Its size depends on the resolver's cache.

::: {#exm-rtt-dns}
#### An uncached name

A resolver $10\,\mathrm{ms}$ away with the record cached answers in $t_D \approx 0$, adding $10\,\mathrm{ms}$. With an
empty cache it must ask a root, a `com` and an authoritative server (@exm-net-dns-hierarchy); if these are $20$, $30$
and $60\,\mathrm{ms}$ away from it, $t_D = 110\,\mathrm{ms}$ and the lookup adds $120\,\mathrm{ms}$, more than the TCP
and TLS handshakes together on a path of $\mathrm{RTT} = 50\,\mathrm{ms}$.
:::

A latency budget of the previous chapter can now be checked against the protocols. The feed's budget gave the network
$80\,\mathrm{ms}$.

::: {#exm-rtt-budget}
#### The network's share of the feed budget

@fig-request-path budgets $80\,\mathrm{ms}$ for the network round trip of a feed request. On a reused connection this
allows $\mathrm{RTT} \leq 80\,\mathrm{ms}$ by part (c); on a new connection with TLS 1.3 the protocol needs $3\,\mathrm{RTT}$
of network time by part (a), so the budget holds only for $\mathrm{RTT} \leq 26.7\,\mathrm{ms}$, that is for users near
the data centre. The budget is therefore a budget for warm connections, and the first request of a session must be
budgeted separately.
:::

An intermediary near the client splits the chain into two. The handshakes then cross only the short part.

::: {#exm-rtt-intermediary}
#### A nearby intermediary

Let a client reach an intermediary at $\mathrm{RTT}_1 = 10\,\mathrm{ms}$, which keeps a persistent connection to the
origin server at $\mathrm{RTT}_2 = 140\,\mathrm{ms}$. A new client connection costs $3\,\mathrm{RTT}_1$ to the moment its
request reaches the intermediary and leaves (part (a) without the response), then the intermediary's request crosses
the warm connection: $T = 3 \times 10 + 140 + t_{\mathrm{srv}} = 170\,\mathrm{ms} + t_{\mathrm{srv}}$, against $3 \times
150 + t_{\mathrm{srv}} = 450\,\mathrm{ms} + t_{\mathrm{srv}}$ directly. This is the latency argument for terminating
connections near the user.
:::

The TLS 1.3 handshake can take an extra round trip. RFC 8446 describes when.

::: {#exm-rtt-hello-retry}
#### A second ClientHello

If the client's ClientHello carries no key share the server accepts, "the server corrects the mismatch with a
HelloRetryRequest and the client needs to restart the handshake" [@rfc8446, Sec. 2.1]. The chain of part (a) gains one
round trip: $T = 4\,\mathrm{RTT} + t_{\mathrm{srv}}$, as with TLS 1.2. Clients avoid it by sending a share for the group
servers most often choose.
:::

The 0-RTT mode removes a round trip but changes what the request may be. The standard names the price.

::: {#exm-rtt-zero-rtt}
#### Early data

With 0-RTT the client sends its request with the ClientHello of a resumed session, so on a new TCP connection $T =
2\,\mathrm{RTT} + t_{\mathrm{srv}}$. But "there are no guarantees of non-replay between connections" for such data
[@rfc8446, Sec. 2.3]: an attacker who records the first flight can send it again. Only requests whose repetition is
harmless, such as reading a feed page, may safely be sent as early data.
:::

The rule behind the proof, that each triggered message waits for its trigger, can be simulated directly. The simulation
below sends each message of part (a) as soon as its trigger arrives.

::: {#exm-rtt-simulation}
#### A simulated handshake

A SimPy process per endpoint waits for each message and sends the next. With $\mathrm{RTT} = 80\,\mathrm{ms}$ and
$t_{\mathrm{srv}} = 30\,\mathrm{ms}$ the first byte arrives at $270\,\mathrm{ms} = 3 \times 80 + 30$, as part (a) says.

```{.python .run}
import simpy
RTT, T_SRV = 0.080, 0.030
env = simpy.Environment()
to_server, to_client = simpy.Store(env), simpy.Store(env)
log = []
def send(store, message):
    def carry():
        yield env.timeout(RTT / 2)
        store.put(message)
    env.process(carry())
def client():
    send(to_server, "SYN")
    yield to_client.get()                                   # SYN-ACK
    send(to_server, "ACK + ClientHello")
    yield to_client.get()                                   # ServerHello ... Finished
    send(to_server, "Finished + GET /feed")
    yield to_client.get()
    log.append(("first byte of the response", env.now))
def server():
    yield to_server.get(); send(to_client, "SYN-ACK")
    yield to_server.get(); send(to_client, "ServerHello ... Finished")
    yield to_server.get(); yield env.timeout(T_SRV); send(to_client, "200 OK")
env.process(client()); env.process(server()); env.run()
for what, t in log:
    print(f"{what}: {t * 1000:.0f} ms (3 RTT + t_srv = {(3 * RTT + T_SRV) * 1000:.0f} ms)")
```

```{.text .run-output}
first byte of the response: 270 ms (3 RTT + t_srv = 270 ms)
```
:::

The last example applies part (d) to a mobile client, which pays for everything at once.

::: {#exm-rtt-mobile}
#### A cold start on a phone

A phone with $\mathrm{RTT} = 100\,\mathrm{ms}$ to the service and $40\,\mathrm{ms}$ to its resolver, whose cache holds
the record, opens the app and loads the feed with $t_{\mathrm{srv}} = 40\,\mathrm{ms}$: $T = 40 + 3 \times 100 + 40 =
380\,\mathrm{ms}$ by parts (a) and (d). Later feed pages on the same connection take $140\,\mathrm{ms}$ by part (c).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise tabulates the four parts of the proposition. It shows how fast the protocols' share grows with
distance.

::: {#exr-rtt-table}
#### A table of first-byte times

For $t_{\mathrm{srv}} = 20\,\mathrm{ms}$ and round-trip times of $1$, $20$, $80$ and $150\,\mathrm{ms}$, give $T$ for a
reused connection, a new TLS 1.3 connection and a new TLS 1.2 connection, and the share of $T$ spent in handshakes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

By parts (c), (a) and (b), $T = \mathrm{RTT} + 20$, $3\,\mathrm{RTT} + 20$ and $4\,\mathrm{RTT} + 20$ milliseconds. The
handshakes take $2\,\mathrm{RTT}$ or $3\,\mathrm{RTT}$ of these: at $1\,\mathrm{ms}$ they are $9\%$ and $12\%$ of $T$, at
$150\,\mathrm{ms}$ they are $64\%$ and $73\%$.

## Python

The table.

```{.python .run}
t_srv = 20
print(" RTT  reused  TLS1.3  TLS1.2  handshake share (1.3, 1.2)")
for rtt in (1, 20, 80, 150):
    reused, tls13, tls12 = rtt + t_srv, 3 * rtt + t_srv, 4 * rtt + t_srv
    print(f"{rtt:4d} {reused:7d} {tls13:7d} {tls12:7d}   {2 * rtt / tls13:.0%}, {3 * rtt / tls12:.0%}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
 RTT  reused  TLS1.3  TLS1.2  handshake share (1.3, 1.2)
   1      21      23      24   9%, 12%
  20      40      80     100   50%, 60%
  80     100     260     340   62%, 71%
 150     170     470     620   64%, 73%
```
::::
:::

The second exercise asks for the TLS 1.2 chain with a message-by-message timeline. It is part (b) written out.

::: {#exr-rtt-tls12-timeline}
#### The TLS 1.2 timeline

List the messages of a new HTTPS request with TLS 1.2, as in the full handshake of RFC 5246 [@rfc5246, Sec. 7.3, Figure 1], with the time at which each arrives
in units of $\mathrm{RTT}$, assuming immediate sending, and confirm part (b).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

SYN arrives at $\tfrac12$, SYN-ACK at $1$, ACK with ClientHello at $\tfrac32$; ServerHello, Certificate and
ServerHelloDone at $2$; ClientKeyExchange, ChangeCipherSpec and Finished at $\tfrac52$; the server's ChangeCipherSpec and
Finished at $3$; the request at $\tfrac72$; the response's first byte at $4\,\mathrm{RTT} + t_{\mathrm{srv}}$. Each
message is triggered by the one before it in the list, which alternates direction, so by the argument of the proof the
times are exact for immediate sending and lower bounds otherwise.

## Python

The timeline generated from the list of messages.

```{.python .run}
messages = ["SYN", "SYN-ACK", "ACK + ClientHello", "ServerHello, Certificate, ServerHelloDone",
            "ClientKeyExchange, ChangeCipherSpec, Finished", "ChangeCipherSpec, Finished", "GET /feed",
            "first byte of the response (+ t_srv)"]
for k, m in enumerate(messages, start=1):
    print(f"{k / 2:.1f} RTT  {'->' if k % 2 else '<-'}  {m}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
0.5 RTT  ->  SYN
1.0 RTT  <-  SYN-ACK
1.5 RTT  ->  ACK + ClientHello
2.0 RTT  <-  ServerHello, Certificate, ServerHelloDone
2.5 RTT  ->  ClientKeyExchange, ChangeCipherSpec, Finished
3.0 RTT  <-  ChangeCipherSpec, Finished
3.5 RTT  ->  GET /feed
4.0 RTT  <-  first byte of the response (+ t_srv)
```
::::
:::

The third exercise uses part (c) to decide how many requests make connection reuse worthwhile. It is the amortisation
of the handshake.

::: {#exr-rtt-amortise}
#### Amortising the handshake

A client sends $k$ requests one after another to a server at $\mathrm{RTT} = 150\,\mathrm{ms}$ with $t_{\mathrm{srv}} =
10\,\mathrm{ms}$. Give the mean time per request with one persistent TLS 1.3 connection and with a new connection per
request, and the smallest $k$ for which the mean with reuse is within $10\%$ of $\mathrm{RTT} + t_{\mathrm{srv}}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

With reuse the total is $2\,\mathrm{RTT} + k(\mathrm{RTT} + t_{\mathrm{srv}})$, so the mean is $\mathrm{RTT} +
t_{\mathrm{srv}} + 2\,\mathrm{RTT}/k = 160 + 300/k$ milliseconds; without reuse it is $3\,\mathrm{RTT} +
t_{\mathrm{srv}} = 460\,\mathrm{ms}$ for every $k$. The mean is within $10\%$ of $160\,\mathrm{ms}$ when $300/k \leq 16$,
that is $k \geq 19$.

## Python

The means and the threshold.

```{.python .run}
from math import ceil
rtt, t_srv = 150, 10
for k in (1, 2, 5, 19, 100):
    print(f"k = {k:3d}: reuse {rtt + t_srv + 2 * rtt / k:6.1f} ms, new connections {3 * rtt + t_srv} ms")
print("smallest k within 10%:", ceil(2 * rtt / (0.1 * (rtt + t_srv))))
```

```{.text .run-output}
k =   1: reuse  460.0 ms, new connections 460 ms
k =   2: reuse  310.0 ms, new connections 460 ms
k =   5: reuse  220.0 ms, new connections 460 ms
k =  19: reuse  175.8 ms, new connections 460 ms
k = 100: reuse  163.0 ms, new connections 460 ms
smallest k within 10%: 19
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise is a page with many resources, loaded over several connections at once. It combines parts (a) and
(c).

::: {#exr-rtt-parallel-connections}
#### Six connections for a page

A browser loads a page that needs $24$ resources after the HTML. It opens six TLS 1.3 connections in parallel at time
$0$ and sends the resources' requests one after another on each, four per connection; $\mathrm{RTT} = 60\,\mathrm{ms}$,
the server's time is $5\,\mathrm{ms}$, and transfer times are neglected. When does the last resource arrive, and how
does this compare with one connection for all $24$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Each connection is ready after $2\,\mathrm{RTT}$ and then carries four requests of $\mathrm{RTT} + 5\,\mathrm{ms}$
each: $2 \times 60 + 4 \times 65 = 380\,\mathrm{ms}$. One connection needs $120 + 24 \times 65 = 1680\,\mathrm{ms}$.
Parallel connections pay the handshake six times but in parallel, and divide the sequential requests by six.

## Python

The two completion times.

```{.python .run}
from math import ceil
rtt, t_srv, resources = 60, 5, 24
for connections in (1, 6):
    print(f"{connections} connection(s): {2 * rtt + ceil(resources / connections) * (rtt + t_srv)} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
1 connection(s): 1680 ms
6 connection(s): 380 ms
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise refines part (d) for an empty cache. The resolver walks the hierarchy one level at a time.

::: {#exr-rtt-iterative-walk}
#### Walking the hierarchy

Prove that if a resolver with an empty cache must query a root, a top-level domain and an authoritative server in turn,
at round-trip times $r_1$, $r_2$ and $r_3$ from it, each answering immediately, then part (d) holds with $t_D = r_1 + r_2 +
r_3$. Compute the time to the first byte for a client at $\mathrm{RTT}_D = 15\,\mathrm{ms}$ from its resolver, $r =
(25, 35, 70)\,\mathrm{ms}$, $\mathrm{RTT} = 50\,\mathrm{ms}$ and $t_{\mathrm{srv}} = 20\,\mathrm{ms}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The resolver learns the address of the next server to ask only from the previous answer, so each query is triggered by
the previous answer; the three exchanges are sequential and take $r_1 + r_2 + r_3$ from the arrival of the client's query
to the resolver's answer, which is $t_D$ in part (d). Then $T = 15 + 130 + 3 \times 50 + 20 = 315\,\mathrm{ms}$, of which
the lookup is $145\,\mathrm{ms}$.

## Python

The sum.

```{.python .run}
rtt_d, r, rtt, t_srv = 15, (25, 35, 70), 50, 20
lookup = rtt_d + sum(r)
print(f"lookup {lookup} ms, first byte at {lookup + 3 * rtt + t_srv} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
lookup 145 ms, first byte at 315 ms
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise drops the assumption that no message is lost. A lost SYN is retransmitted after a timeout.

::: {#exr-rtt-lost-syn}
#### A lost SYN

Suppose each of the client's SYNs is lost independently with probability $\pi$ and the client resends it after a fixed
retransmission timeout of $1\,\mathrm{s}$ (an assumption of the exercise), everything else as in part (a). Give the
expected time to the first byte, and evaluate it for $\pi = 0.01$ and $0.05$, $\mathrm{RTT} = 80\,\mathrm{ms}$ and
$t_{\mathrm{srv}} = 20\,\mathrm{ms}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The number of lost SYNs before the first that arrives is $K - 1$ with $K$ geometric with parameter $1 - \pi$
([geometric distribution](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#def-binomial-distribution)),
so its mean is $\pi/(1 - \pi)$ and the expected time is $3\,\mathrm{RTT} + t_{\mathrm{srv}} + \pi/(1 - \pi) \times
1\,\mathrm{s}$: $260 + 10.1 = 270.1\,\mathrm{ms}$ for $\pi = 0.01$ and $260 + 52.6 = 312.6\,\mathrm{ms}$ for $\pi = 0.05$.
The mean hides the tail: with probability $\pi$ the request takes more than a second.

## Python

The formula and a seeded simulation.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
rtt, t_srv, rto = 0.080, 0.020, 1.0
for pi in (0.01, 0.05):
    losses = rng.geometric(1 - pi, 200_000) - 1
    sim = 3 * rtt + t_srv + rto * losses
    print(f"pi = {pi}: expected {(3 * rtt + t_srv + rto * pi / (1 - pi)) * 1000:.1f} ms, "
          f"simulated {sim.mean() * 1000:.1f} ms, P(T > 1 s) = {np.mean(sim > 1):.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
pi = 0.01: expected 270.1 ms, simulated 270.4 ms, P(T > 1 s) = 0.010
pi = 0.05: expected 312.6 ms, simulated 312.6 ms, P(T > 1 s) = 0.050
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise inverts part (a) to give the largest distance a budget allows. It uses the speed of light in fibre
of @exr-req-light-bound.

::: {#exr-rtt-distance}
#### How far may the user be?

A product requires the first feed page of a new session within $300\,\mathrm{ms}$, with $t_{\mathrm{srv}} =
40\,\mathrm{ms}$ and the name cached. Give the largest round-trip time allowed with TLS 1.3 and with TLS 1.2, and the
largest distance at $2 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{km/s}$ in fibre along a straight path.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Part (a) needs $3\,\mathrm{RTT} \leq 260\,\mathrm{ms}$, so $\mathrm{RTT} \leq 86.7\,\mathrm{ms}$; part (b) needs
$\mathrm{RTT} \leq 65\,\mathrm{ms}$. A round trip covers twice the distance, so the distance is at most $\mathrm{RTT}
\times 10^5\,\mathrm{km/s}$: $8667\,\mathrm{km}$ and $6500\,\mathrm{km}$. Real paths are longer and slower, so these are
upper bounds.

## Python

The two limits.

```{.python .run}
budget, t_srv, c_fibre = 300, 40, 2e5                       # ms, ms, km/s
for name, k in (("TLS 1.3", 3), ("TLS 1.2", 4)):
    rtt = (budget - t_srv) / k
    print(f"{name}: RTT <= {rtt:.1f} ms, distance <= {rtt / 1000 * c_fibre / 2:,.0f} km")
```

```{.text .run-output}
TLS 1.3: RTT <= 86.7 ms, distance <= 8,667 km
TLS 1.2: RTT <= 65.0 ms, distance <= 6,500 km
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise changes the simulation of @exm-rtt-simulation. It checks part (b) the same way.

::: {#exr-rtt-simulate-tls12}
#### Simulating TLS 1.2

Change the simulation of @exm-rtt-simulation to the TLS 1.2 handshake and confirm $T = 4\,\mathrm{RTT} +
t_{\mathrm{srv}}$ for $\mathrm{RTT} = 80\,\mathrm{ms}$ and $t_{\mathrm{srv}} = 30\,\mathrm{ms}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The client waits for one more message (the server's Finished) after sending its key exchange; the server answers that
flight before it receives the request. The first byte arrives at $4 \times 80 + 30 = 350\,\mathrm{ms}$.

## Python

The same processes with one more exchange.

```{.python .run}
import simpy
RTT, T_SRV = 0.080, 0.030
env = simpy.Environment()
to_server, to_client = simpy.Store(env), simpy.Store(env)
arrival = {}
def send(store, message):
    def carry():
        yield env.timeout(RTT / 2)
        store.put(message)
    env.process(carry())
def client():
    send(to_server, "SYN")
    for message in ("ACK + ClientHello", "ClientKeyExchange + Finished", "GET /feed"):
        yield to_client.get()
        send(to_server, message)
    yield to_client.get()
    arrival["first byte"] = env.now
def server():
    for reply in ("SYN-ACK", "ServerHello ... ServerHelloDone", "Finished"):
        yield to_server.get()
        send(to_client, reply)
    yield to_server.get(); yield env.timeout(T_SRV); send(to_client, "200 OK")
env.process(client()); env.process(server()); env.run()
print(f"first byte at {arrival['first byte'] * 1000:.0f} ms; 4 RTT + t_srv = {(4 * RTT + T_SRV) * 1000:.0f} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
first byte at 350 ms; 4 RTT + t_srv = 350 ms
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise proves the formula of @exm-rtt-intermediary. An intermediary that keeps its connection to the origin
open removes the handshakes from the long part of the path.

::: {#exr-rtt-intermediary-proof}
#### The intermediary's chain

Let a client reach an intermediary at $\mathrm{RTT}_1$, which holds an established persistent connection to the origin
at $\mathrm{RTT}_2$ and forwards a request as soon as it has received it, and the response's first byte as soon as it
has received it. Prove that a new TLS 1.3 client connection gives $T = 3\,\mathrm{RTT}_1 + \mathrm{RTT}_2 +
t_{\mathrm{srv}}$ under the hypotheses of the proposition, and that this is smaller than $3(\mathrm{RTT}_1 +
\mathrm{RTT}_2) + t_{\mathrm{srv}}$ whenever $\mathrm{RTT}_2 > 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By the chain of part (a) applied to the client and the intermediary, the request reaches the intermediary at
$\tfrac52\mathrm{RTT}_1$. It crosses the warm connection in $\mathrm{RTT}_2/2$, the origin answers after
$t_{\mathrm{srv}}$, the first byte crosses back in $\mathrm{RTT}_2/2$ and then to the client in $\mathrm{RTT}_1/2$: $T =
\tfrac52\mathrm{RTT}_1 + \mathrm{RTT}_2 + t_{\mathrm{srv}} + \tfrac12\mathrm{RTT}_1 = 3\,\mathrm{RTT}_1 + \mathrm{RTT}_2
+ t_{\mathrm{srv}}$. The difference from the direct connection over a path of $\mathrm{RTT}_1 + \mathrm{RTT}_2$ is
$2\,\mathrm{RTT}_2 > 0$.

## Python

The two times for a few splits of a $150\,\mathrm{ms}$ path.

```{.python .run}
t_srv = 20
for rtt1 in (5, 10, 30, 75):
    rtt2 = 150 - rtt1
    print(f"RTT1 = {rtt1:3d}, RTT2 = {rtt2:3d}: via intermediary {3 * rtt1 + rtt2 + t_srv} ms, direct {3 * 150 + t_srv} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
RTT1 =   5, RTT2 = 145: via intermediary 180 ms, direct 470 ms
RTT1 =  10, RTT2 = 140: via intermediary 190 ms, direct 470 ms
RTT1 =  30, RTT2 = 120: via intermediary 230 ms, direct 470 ms
RTT1 =  75, RTT2 =  75: via intermediary 320 ms, direct 470 ms
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise uses the proposition to judge a design. The question is whether a feed should be split into several
calls.

::: {#exr-rtt-chatty}
#### A chatty client

A mobile client at $\mathrm{RTT} = 100\,\mathrm{ms}$ builds its feed screen from three calls that must be made in turn
(the user profile, then the list of photo identifiers, then the photos' metadata), each with $t_{\mathrm{srv}} =
15\,\mathrm{ms}$, on a new TLS 1.3 connection. A single combined call would take $t_{\mathrm{srv}} = 35\,\mathrm{ms}$.
Compare the times to the full screen.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Three sequential calls: $2\,\mathrm{RTT}$ of handshakes and then three request round trips, $200 + 3 \times 115 =
545\,\mathrm{ms}$. One call: $3 \times 100 + 35 = 335\,\mathrm{ms}$. Each round trip saved is worth more than the extra
server work.

## Python

The two totals.

```{.python .run}
rtt = 100
print("three calls:", 2 * rtt + 3 * (rtt + 15), "ms; one call:", 3 * rtt + 35, "ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
three calls: 545 ms; one call: 335 ms
```
::::
:::
::::

## Load balancing {#sec-load-balancing}

One server is a single point of failure and has a fixed capacity. Xu's remedy is the first component he adds to the
single-server design: "A load balancer evenly distributes incoming traffic among web servers that are defined in a
load-balanced set" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 1, "Load balancer"], and Tan notes that "every horizontally scaled
service uses a load balancer" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 3.1.2, p. 57]. A load balancer is an intermediary in the
sense of @def-request-path. This section defines what it does, at which layer, by which rules and with which checks of
its servers, and then proves how evenly the two simplest rules, round robin and random choice, spread requests. The
stronger rules that look at the servers' loads are compared by simulation, and the classical result on two random
choices is quoted.

For more on this topic, see @sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024 [Ch. 4, "Load balancers"], @tanAcingSystemDesign2024
[Sec. 3.1.2], @SystemDesignInterview2021 [Ch. 1], @liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 5, "Service Discovery and Request
Routing"] and @mitzenmacher2001power [Sec. 1].

### Load balancers

Sinha and Chopra describe a load balancer by where it is placed, which layer it reads, which algorithm it applies and
how it learns which servers are healthy [@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 4, "Load balancers"]. The definition keeps
these four parts and adds the global level, which chooses a data centre before a local balancer chooses a server.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-load-balancer}
#### Load balancer

A **load balancer** for a **pool** of servers $1, \dots, n$ is an intermediary that receives the requests addressed to
one service address and forwards each to one server of the pool.

1. (**Layer**) A **layer-4** balancer decides once per TCP connection, from the addresses and ports of its first
   packets, and forwards the connection's bytes unread. A **layer-7** balancer terminates the connection (and usually
   TLS), reads each HTTP request and decides per request, from its method, path, header fields or cookies.
2. (**Assignment rule**) The server for the next request (or connection) is chosen by a rule. **Static** rules ignore
   the servers' state: **round robin** takes servers $1, 2, \dots, n, 1, 2, \dots$ in turn; **weighted round robin**
   gives server $j$ a share $w_j/\sum_iw_i$ of the requests; **random** choice picks a server uniformly at random;
   **hashing** picks server $g(x) \bmod n + 1$ for a hash $g$ of a request attribute $x$ (the client's address, a cookie,
   the URL). **Dynamic** rules use the state: **least connections** picks a server with the fewest requests in
   progress, and the **power of $d$ choices** picks $d$ servers at random and sends the request to the one of them with
   the fewest requests in progress.
3. (**Health checks**) The balancer probes each server every $\Delta_h$ seconds and forwards only to servers it marks
   healthy; a server is marked down after $k$ consecutive failed probes and up again after a given number of successes.
4. (**Global load balancing**) Before any local balancer, a **global** balancer chooses the data centre, by the answer
   of DNS (@exm-net-geodns) or by anycast routing (@exm-net-anycast), using the health and capacity of the data centres.
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Xu's first use of a load balancer shows the two benefits at once: more capacity and no single server whose failure
stops the service.

::: {#exm-lb-xu-pool}
#### Two web servers behind one address

In Xu's design "users connect to the public IP of the load balancer directly", servers are reached only by private
addresses, and "if server 1 goes offline, all the traffic will be routed to server 2"; to grow, "you only need to add
more servers to the web server pool" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 1, "Load balancer"]. The pool is $\{1, 2\}$, the
service address is the balancer's public address, and the failover is the health check of item 3.
:::

Load balancers are not only at the entrance. Sinha and Chopra place them between any two tiers.

::: {#exm-lb-placement}
#### Where balancers sit

Load balancers can be placed "between clients and frontend servers, between different tiers of a multi-tier system,
and potentially between any two services with multiple instances" [@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 4, "Placing load
balancers"]. In the photo service of @fig-three-tier one balancer spreads client requests over the $146$ application
servers, and the application servers' calls to the cache and database replicas are spread by another, so that each tier
"can be scaled independently".
:::

The two layers of item 1 differ in what they can see. Tan lists what a layer-7 balancer can do that a layer-4 one cannot.

::: {#exm-lb-l4-l7}
#### Layer 4 against layer 7

A layer-4 balancer "makes routing decisions based on address information extracted from the first few packets in the
TCP stream and does not inspect the contents of other packets"; a layer-7 balancer can route "based on a packet's
contents" and can reject a request: "it can return 401 if a specified authentication header is absent"
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 3.1.2, pp. 57-58]. Sinha and Chopra add that layer-4 balancers "tend to be faster since
they operate at a lower level" [@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 4, "Load balancing at different layers of the Open
Systems Interconnection (OSI) model"]. Sending `/upload` and `/feed` to different pools needs layer 7.
:::

A layer-7 balancer must decrypt to read the request. Where it does so is a security decision as well as a performance
one.

::: {#exm-lb-tls-termination}
#### TLS termination

With TLS termination "there is no encryption/decryption overhead between data center hosts", but "if our application
requires traffic within our data center to be encrypted (i.e., encryption in transit), we will not do TLS termination"
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 3.1.2, p. 58]; in practice the balancer then opens a second TLS connection to the
server. Either way the client's handshakes of @prp-net-round-trips end at the balancer, which is usually closer to the
client than the servers are.
:::

Weights express unequal capacities. A pool that mixes machine sizes needs them, or the small machines saturate first.

::: {#exm-lb-weighted}
#### Weights for a mixed pool

A feed pool has two servers of capacity $2000$ requests per second and one of $4000$. Weights $1 : 1 : 2$ send a quarter,
a quarter and a half of the requests to them, so all three reach the same fraction of their capacity together; with
plain round robin the small servers are full when the pool carries $6000$ requests per second, three quarters of its
capacity of $8000$.
:::

Least connections responds to requests of unequal cost. Sinha and Chopra say why it helps.

::: {#exm-lb-least-connections}
#### Least connections

Least connections "helps distribute load more evenly among servers, especially when some requests take longer to serve",
at the price that "the load balancer must track the number of connections to each server"
[@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 4, "Load balancer algorithms"]. A server stuck on a slow request keeps a high count and
receives no new requests until it finishes, which round robin cannot notice.
:::

Health checks take time to notice a failure. The time, multiplied by the request rate, is the number of requests that
fail meanwhile.

::: {#exm-lb-health-checks}
#### Detecting a dead server

With probes every $\Delta_h = 5\,\mathrm{s}$ and $k = 3$ failures to mark a server down, a server that dies just after a
successful probe is detected after up to $15\,\mathrm{s}$. During that time it receives its share of the feed's peak,
$1.74 \times 10^5/146 = 1192$ requests per second, and about $1.8 \times 10^4$ requests fail. Retrying such requests on
another server hides the failure from users, which is safe for reads.
:::

Global load balancing is the first decision of the path. @fig-lb-topology shows it above two data centres, each with
layer-4 and layer-7 balancers.

::: {#exm-lb-gslb}
#### Global and local balancing

Global balancing "distributes traffic across data centers in different geographical regions", and "the local load
balancers report health and capacity information to the GSLB" [@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 4, "Global and local
load balancing"]. Done through DNS it is coarse: "the small 512-byte size of DNS packets means DNS cannot include all
possible server IP addresses", clients pick arbitrarily among the addresses returned, and "recovery through DNS can be
slow due to caching" [@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 4, "DNS and GSLB"]; the limit is that of RFC 1035, "UDP messages
512 octets or less" [@rfc1035, Sec. 2.3.4].

![Global load balancing chooses a data centre; in each, layer-4 balancers spread connections over layer-7 balancers,
which spread requests over the application servers.](figures/lb_topology.svg){#fig-lb-topology width=75%}
:::

Large deployments stack the layers. Sinha and Chopra describe four tiers.

::: {#exm-lb-tiers}
#### Tiers of balancing

"Tier 0 uses the DNS system to switch between multiple IP addresses", tier 1 uses routers that split traffic by address
or round robin, "Tier 2 uses Layer 4 load balancers to make sure that all pieces of data related to a single online
activity go to the same next-level load balancer", and tier 3 uses layer-7 balancers that check the servers' health
[@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 4, "Deployment of load balancers"]. In @fig-lb-topology tier 0 is the global
balancer, tier 2 the layer-4 boxes and tier 3 the layer-7 boxes; each tier can grow without the others noticing.
:::

A software balancer is configured by a short file. The configuration below is illustrative: it would need a running
server and is not run.

::: {#exm-lb-nginx}
#### A balancer's configuration

Tan names HAProxy and NGINX as "the most common" software balancers [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 3.1.2, p. 57]. A
configuration for the feed pool of @exm-lb-weighted states the layer (an HTTP server that terminates TLS), the rule
(least connections), the weights and a passive health check that stops using a server after three failures within
$15\,\mathrm{s}$:

```{.code .illustrative}
# Illustrative: an nginx configuration for a layer-7 balancer; not run, no recorded output.
upstream feed {
    least_conn;
    server 10.0.1.11:8080 weight=1 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=15s;
    server 10.0.1.12:8080 weight=1 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=15s;
    server 10.0.1.13:8080 weight=2 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=15s;
}
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name photos.example.com;
    ssl_certificate     /etc/nginx/tls/photos.crt;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/nginx/tls/photos.key;
    location /feed   { proxy_pass http://feed; }
    location /upload { proxy_pass http://upload; }
}
```

The two `location` blocks are layer-7 routing by path; a layer-4 balancer could not separate them.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise implements weighted round robin so that heavy servers do not receive their requests in bursts. It
uses the "smooth" variant, which interleaves.

::: {#exr-lb-smooth-wrr}
#### Smooth weighted round robin

Each server $j$ has a weight $w_j$ and a counter $c_j$, initially $0$. For each request every counter is increased by its
weight, the server with the largest counter is chosen (the first in case of ties), and its counter is decreased by $W =
\sum_jw_j$. For weights $(5, 1, 1)$ list the first $14$ choices and the counts per server. How does the sequence differ
from sending five requests in a row to the first server?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The counters always sum to $0$ after a choice, since $W$ is added and $W$ subtracted. The rule chooses `a a b a c a a`
and then repeats, so every block of seven requests carries five to the first server and one to each other, as the
weights ask, but the heavy server never receives more than two in a row and the light servers are served in the middle
of the block rather than after a burst of five.

## Python

The rule for $(5, 1, 1)$.

```{.python .run}
weights = {"a": 5, "b": 1, "c": 1}
counter = {k: 0 for k in weights}
total, choices = sum(weights.values()), []
for _ in range(14):
    for k in counter:
        counter[k] += weights[k]
    best = max(counter, key=lambda k: counter[k])           # first maximum in case of ties
    counter[best] -= total
    choices.append(best)
print(" ".join(choices))
print({k: choices.count(k) for k in weights})
```

```{.text .run-output}
a a b a c a a a a b a c a a
{'a': 10, 'b': 2, 'c': 2}
```
::::
:::

The second exercise shows the weakness of hashing modulo the pool size. Adding one server moves almost every key.

::: {#exr-lb-modulo-rehash}
#### Adding a server under modular hashing

A balancer sends each client to server $g(x) \bmod n$ (numbering servers from $0$), where $g(x)$ is uniformly
distributed on $\{0, 1, \dots, L - 1\}$ and $L$ is a multiple of $n(n + 1)$. Prove that when the pool grows from $n$ to $n
+ 1$ servers, a client keeps its server with probability exactly $1/(n + 1)$. What fraction of clients moves when the
feed pool grows from $146$ to $147$ servers?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Both residues are periodic with period $n(n + 1)$, so it suffices to count the values $v \in \{0, \dots, n(n + 1) - 1\}$
with $v \bmod n = v \bmod (n + 1)$. Write $v = q(n + 1) + r$ with $0 \leq r \leq n$ and $0 \leq q \leq n - 1$. Then $v
\bmod (n + 1) = r$ and $v \equiv q + r \pmod n$. If $q \geq 1$, then $1 \leq q \leq n - 1$ and $q + r \not\equiv r
\pmod n$, so the residues differ. If $q = 0$, then $v = r$, and $v \bmod n = r$ exactly when $r < n$. The values that keep
their server are $0, 1, \dots, n - 1$: $n$ of the $n(n + 1)$, a fraction $1/(n + 1)$. Growing from $146$ to $147$ servers
moves $146/147 = 99.3\%$ of the clients.

## Python

The fraction from the proof, and the fraction of $10^5$ hashed client identifiers that change server.

```{.python .run}
import hashlib
n = 146
keys = [f"client-{i}" for i in range(100_000)]
g = [int.from_bytes(hashlib.sha256(k.encode()).digest()[:8], "big") for k in keys]
stay = sum(v % n == v % (n + 1) for v in g) / len(g)
print(f"predicted stay {1 / (n + 1):.4f}, observed {stay:.4f}; moved {1 - stay:.1%}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
predicted stay 0.0068, observed 0.0067; moved 99.3%
```
::::
:::

The third exercise chooses the number of failed probes. Fewer failures detect dead servers faster but also mark healthy
servers down after a few lost probes.

::: {#exr-lb-probe-count}
