Each insertion moves the items of page $i$ and all later items one position up, so $r$ insertions move them $r$ positions.
Positions $(i + 1)b + 1, \dots, (i + 1)b + r$ now hold the items that were at $(i + 1)b - r + 1, \dots, (i + 1)b$, the
last $r$ of page $i$. For $r > b$ the positions of page $i + 1$ hold items that were at positions $(i + 1)b - r + 1,
\dots, (i + 2)b - r$, all at most $(i + 1)b$; each item of page $i + 1$ is either one of the inserted items or an item already read, and the
traversal makes no progress through the old list.

## Python

The repeats for $r = 0, \dots, 12$ with $b = 10$, by direct listing.

```{.python .run}
b = 10
for r in (0, 1, 3, 10, 12):
    items = list(range(100, 0, -1))                  # newest first: position 1 holds 100
    page0 = items[:b]
    items = list(range(100 + r, 100, -1)) + items     # r new items at the front
    page1 = items[b:2 * b]
    print(f"r = {r:2d}: repeated {len(set(page0) & set(page1))}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
r =  0: repeated 0
r =  1: repeated 1
r =  3: repeated 3
r = 10: repeated 10
r = 12: repeated 8
```
::::
:::

The third exercise implements the composite key of @exm-page-ties in SQL. SQLite compares row values lexicographically.

::: {#exr-page-composite}
#### A composite cursor

A feed table has columns (time, id) with many equal times. Write the keyset query with the condition `(time, id) < (?,
?)` ordered by time and id descending, and check with `sqlite3` that a traversal with pages of $3$ returns every row once,
while the condition `time < ?` on the time alone loses rows.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The pair (time, id) is unique and ordered lexicographically, so part (a) applies to it. With the time alone the keys are
not distinct: a page that ends in the middle of a group of equal times leaves the rest of the group behind, because the
next page asks for times strictly below the cursor.

## Python

The two traversals over $20$ rows with five distinct times.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE feed(time INTEGER, id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO feed VALUES (?, ?)", [(1000 + i // 4 * 60, i) for i in range(20)])
def traverse(composite):
    seen, cursor = [], (10**9, 10**9)
    while True:
        if composite:
            rows = db.execute("SELECT time, id FROM feed WHERE (time, id) < (?, ?) ORDER BY time DESC, id DESC LIMIT 3",
                              cursor).fetchall()
        else:
            rows = db.execute("SELECT time, id FROM feed WHERE time < ? ORDER BY time DESC, id DESC LIMIT 3",
                              (cursor[0],)).fetchall()
        seen += [r[1] for r in rows]
        if len(rows) < 3:
            return seen
        cursor = rows[-1]
for composite in (True, False):
    seen = traverse(composite)
    print(f"{'(time, id)' if composite else 'time only '}: {len(seen)} rows returned, {len(set(seen))} distinct, of 20")
```

```{.text .run-output}
(time, id): 20 rows returned, 20 distinct, of 20
time only : 15 rows returned, 15 distinct, of 20
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise makes the cursor of @exm-page-opaque-cursor tamper-evident. A client should not be able to forge a
cursor to reach another user's items.

::: {#exr-page-signed-cursor}
#### A signed cursor

Encode a cursor as `base64url(key) "." base64url(HMAC(K, key))[:16]` and write the decoder that rejects a changed key. Is
the signature needed if the server also checks, on every page, that the user may read the items it returns?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The decoder recomputes the HMAC of the decoded key and compares in constant time. If every page is filtered by the user's
permissions, a forged cursor can only move the traversal within what the user may read anyway, so the signature is not
needed for security; it still prevents clients from depending on the cursor's format, which keeps the format free to
change.

## Python

Encoding, decoding and a forged cursor.

```{.python .run}
import base64, hmac, hashlib
K = b"cursor-key"
b64 = lambda b: base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=").decode()
unb64 = lambda s: base64.urlsafe_b64decode(s + "=" * (-len(s) % 4))
def encode(key):
    raw = key.encode()
    return b64(raw) + "." + b64(hmac.new(K, raw, hashlib.sha256).digest())[:16]
def decode(cursor):
    body, sig = cursor.split(".")
    raw = unb64(body)
    if not hmac.compare_digest(sig, b64(hmac.new(K, raw, hashlib.sha256).digest())[:16]):
        raise ValueError("tampered cursor")
    return raw.decode()
c = encode("1790000000:9000000016")
print(c, "->", decode(c))
forged = b64(b"1790000000:9000000999") + "." + c.split(".")[1]
try:
    decode(forged)
except ValueError as e:
    print("forged:", e)
```

```{.text .run-output}
MTc5MDAwMDAwMDo5MDAwMDAwMDE2.rxz8BIgzi8_OAvNX -> 1790000000:9000000016
forged: tampered cursor
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise asks what keyset pagination returns of items inserted during the traversal. Part (a) allows both.

::: {#exr-page-inserted-items}
#### Items that arrive during the traversal

Prove that under keyset pagination in increasing order an item inserted during the traversal and not deleted afterwards
is returned if its key is greater than the cursor of the next page request after its insertion, and is never returned if
its key is smaller.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Let $c$ be the cursor of the next page request after the insertion. Cursors increase strictly, since every key on a
page exceeds the previous cursor. If $k < c$, every later page returns keys above a cursor $\geq c > k$, so $k$ is never
returned. If $k > c$, the item is present at every later request, and the argument of part (a) applies with $c$ in place
of the initial cursor: a first later cursor $\geq k$ would come from a page of $b$ keys smaller than $k$, and if there is
none, the last page returns every present key above its cursor, including $k$.

## Python

An item inserted below and one above the cursor during a traversal.

```{.python .run}
items, b, cursor, seen = set(range(0, 100, 5)), 4, -1, []
step = 0
while True:
    page = sorted(k for k in items if k > cursor)[:b]
    seen += page
    if len(page) < b:
        break
    cursor = page[-1]; step += 1
    if step == 2:
        items |= {1, 101}                             # 1 is below the cursor 35, 101 above everything
print("cursor when inserted: 35 | 1 returned:", 1 in seen, "| 101 returned:", 101 in seen)
```

```{.text .run-output}
cursor when inserted: 35 | 1 returned: False | 101 returned: True
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise checks that offset pagination fails in the way part (b) predicts, on random changes. The counts of
repeats and misses should match the insertions and deletions before the current page.

::: {#exr-page-offset-random}
#### Offset pagination on random changes

Repeat the simulation of @exm-page-simulation with offset pages, inserting keys below the current page only, and count
repeats; then delete keys from pages already read only, and count misses of items that stayed. Compare with the numbers of
insertions and deletions.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

By part (b) and @exr-page-many-inserts, each insertion before the current position causes one repeat (as long as fewer
than $b$ arrive between two pages), and each deletion before it causes one miss. The simulation counts exactly as many
repeats as insertions and misses as deletions.

## Python

Two runs of $1000$ traversals each.

```{.python .run}
import random
random.seed(13)
def run(mode, b=7):
    reps = miss = changes = 0
    for _ in range(1000):
        items = sorted(random.sample(range(0, 20_000, 2), 100)); stayed = set(items); seen = []; i = 0
        while True:
            page = items[i * b:(i + 1) * b]; seen += page
            if len(page) < b:
                break
            if mode == "insert":                       # two new odd keys below the page just read
                present, new = set(items), []
                for _ in range(50 if page[0] > 1 else 0):            # up to two new odd keys below the page
                    if len(new) == 2:
                        break
                    k = 2 * random.randrange(page[0] // 2) + 1
                    if k < page[0] and k not in present and k not in new:
                        new.append(k)
                items = sorted(items + new); changes += len(new)
            else:                                      # two deletions among the items already read
                seen_set = set(seen)
                read = [k for k in items[:(i + 1) * b] if k in seen_set]
                for k in random.sample(read, min(2, len(read))):
                    items.remove(k); stayed.discard(k); changes += 1
            i += 1
        reps += len(seen) - len(set(seen)); miss += len(stayed - set(seen))
    return reps, miss, changes
print("insertions below the page: repeats %d, misses %d, insertions %d" % run("insert"))
print("deletions of read items:   repeats %d, misses %d, deletions %d" % run("delete"))
```

```{.text .run-output}
insertions below the page: repeats 37973, misses 0, insertions 37973
deletions of read items:   repeats 0, misses 22000, deletions 22000
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise bounds the length of a keyset traversal. Insertions above the cursor can lengthen it without
limit.

::: {#exr-page-termination}
#### Does the traversal end?

Show that a keyset traversal of a list with $N$ items, during which $I$ items are inserted in total, requests at most
$\lfloor(N + I)/b\rfloor + 1$ pages. Give an insertion pattern under which the traversal never ends, and say why it does
not contradict part (a).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

By part (a) every item is returned at most once, and every page but the last is full, so the full pages return at most $N
+ I$ distinct items: at most $\lfloor(N + I)/b\rfloor$ full pages and one more. If $b$ new items with keys above every key
arrive before each page request, every page is full and the traversal never stops; part (a) is a statement about the items
returned, and it is still true that none repeats. A client therefore also stops at a page count or at a key fixed at the
start.

## Python

The bound for a few values, and a traversal with a stop key fixed at the start.

```{.python .run}
for N, I, b in ((100, 0, 10), (100, 25, 10), (95, 0, 10)):
    print(f"N = {N}, I = {I}, b = {b}: at most {(N + I) // b + 1} pages")
items, cursor, stop, pages = set(range(30)), -1, 29, 0
while True:
    page = sorted(k for k in items if cursor < k <= stop)[:10]; pages += 1
    items |= set(range(1000 + 10 * pages, 1010 + 10 * pages))     # ten new keys above everything
    if len(page) < 10:
        break
    cursor = page[-1]
print("pages with a stop key:", pages)
```

```{.text .run-output}
N = 100, I = 0, b = 10: at most 11 pages
N = 100, I = 25, b = 10: at most 13 pages
N = 95, I = 0, b = 10: at most 10 pages
pages with a stop key: 4
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise compares the cost of deep pages. An offset query reads every skipped row.

::: {#exr-page-depth-cost}
#### Deep pages

Count the rows that `sqlite3` visits for page $i$ of an offset query and of a keyset query on an indexed key, for $i = 0,
10, 100, 1000$ with $b = 10$, using the virtual-machine step counter of a progress handler as a measure of work.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The offset query steps through the $ib$ rows it skips, so its work grows linearly with $i$; the keyset query seeks to the
cursor in the index and reads ten rows, so its work does not depend on $i$. The step counts below show it.

## Python

A progress handler called every virtual-machine instruction counts the work of each query.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE feed(photo INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO feed VALUES (?)", [(i,) for i in range(1, 20_001)])
steps = [0]
def count():
    steps[0] += 1
db.set_progress_handler(count, 1)
for i in (0, 10, 100, 1000):
    steps[0] = 0; db.execute("SELECT photo FROM feed ORDER BY photo DESC LIMIT 10 OFFSET ?", (10 * i,)).fetchall()
    offset_steps = steps[0]
    steps[0] = 0; db.execute("SELECT photo FROM feed WHERE photo < ? ORDER BY photo DESC LIMIT 10",
                             (20_001 - 10 * i,)).fetchall()
    print(f"page {i:4d}: offset {offset_steps:7d} steps, keyset {steps[0]:4d} steps")
```

```{.text .run-output}
page    0: offset      60 steps, keyset   49 steps
page   10: offset     260 steps, keyset   48 steps
page  100: offset    2060 steps, keyset   48 steps
page 1000: offset   20060 steps, keyset   48 steps
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise designs the feed's paginated operation completely. It combines item 3 of @def-web-api with the
proposition.

::: {#exr-page-feed-design}
#### The feed's operation

Specify `GET /feed` with keyset pagination for the photo service: its parameters, its response fields, the key, the order,
the meaning of an absent cursor, and what the client does to show photos posted after it started scrolling.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Parameters: `cursor` (opaque, optional) and `limit` (at most $50$). Key: (upload time, photo identifier), newest first.
Without a cursor the first page is the newest $b$ photos. Response: `photos` (at most `limit` items), `next_cursor`
(absent on the last page) and `newest_cursor` (the key of the first item, on the first page). The client scrolls with
`next_cursor`; new photos are fetched with `GET /feed/newer?after=<newest_cursor>`, which returns keys above it. By the
proposition and @exr-page-descending, scrolling never repeats or skips a photo that stays.

## Python

A minimal server for the operation over an in-memory list, with a newer post arriving during scrolling.

```{.python .run}
posts = [(1_790_000_000 + 60 * i, i) for i in range(1, 26)]       # (time, id)
def feed(cursor=None, limit=10):
    rows = sorted((p for p in posts if cursor is None or p < cursor), reverse=True)[:limit]
    return {"photos": [p[1] for p in rows], "next_cursor": rows[-1] if len(rows) == limit else None}
first = feed()
posts.append((1_790_000_000 + 60 * 26, 26))                          # a new post while scrolling
second = feed(first["next_cursor"])
print("page 1:", first["photos"]); print("page 2:", second["photos"])
print("newer:", [p[1] for p in posts if p > (1_790_000_000 + 60 * 25, 25)])
```

```{.text .run-output}
page 1: [25, 24, 23, 22, 21, 20, 19, 18, 17, 16]
page 2: [15, 14, 13, 12, 11, 10, 9, 8, 7, 6]
newer: [26]
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise asks for the guarantee when the key of an item can change. Part (a) assumed fixed keys.

::: {#exr-page-changing-key}
#### When a key changes

A feed ordered by like count, with the photo identifier as tie-breaker, uses keyset pagination. Show by an example that a
photo whose like count increases during the traversal can be returned twice or not at all, and explain this with part (a)
by treating a change of key as a deletion followed by an insertion.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A change of key is the deletion of the item with its old key and the insertion of an item with its new key. Part (a)
promises nothing to items that do not stay throughout. If a photo already returned moves above the cursor (in the
traversal's order), it is inserted where the traversal has yet to go and is returned again; if a photo not yet returned
moves behind the cursor, it is never returned. Pagination by a key that changes needs a snapshot of the order, such as
Tan's page version.

## Python

The two cases in an ascending traversal by (likes, id).

```{.python .run}
likes = {i: 10 * i for i in range(1, 13)}               # photo -> likes
def page(cursor, b=4):
    return sorted((likes[p], p) for p in likes if (likes[p], p) > cursor)[:b]
p1 = page((-1, -1)); cursor = p1[-1]
likes[2] = 1000                                          # photo 2, already returned, moves ahead of the cursor
likes[6] = 5                                             # photo 6, not yet returned, moves behind it
seen = [p for _, p in p1]
while True:
    pg = page(cursor); seen += [p for _, p in pg]
    if len(pg) < 4:
        break
    cursor = pg[-1]
print("returned:", seen, "| photo 2 twice:", seen.count(2) == 2, "| photo 6 missing:", 6 not in seen)
```

```{.text .run-output}
returned: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 2] | photo 2 twice: True | photo 6 missing: True
```
::::
:::
::::

## Real-time delivery {#sec-real-time}

HTTP lets a client ask and a server answer; it gives the server no way to speak first. "In the standard HTTP model, a
server cannot initiate a connection with a client nor send an unrequested HTTP response to a client; thus, the server
cannot push asynchronous events to clients" [@rfc6202, Sec. 1]. Yet a chat message, a notification or a price must reach
the client when it happens. Liu describes the need as "pushing updated events from the servers to the clients"
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Real-Time Data Update"], and Xu lists the techniques used "to simulate a
server-initiated connection: polling, long polling, and WebSocket" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 12, Step 2]. This
section defines the four methods, adds server-sent events, and then proves the delay and the number of requests of each,
which is the trade-off the benchmark books describe in words.

For more on this topic, see @liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 5, "Real-Time Data Update"], @SystemDesignInterview2021
[Ch. 12, Step 2 and "Online presence"], @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Sec. 6.7.5], @rfc6202 [Secs. 1-2], @rfc6455
[Secs. 1.1-1.3 and 5.5] and @whatwgHTML [Sec. 9.2].

### Polling, long polling, server-sent events and WebSocket

The four methods differ in who sends what, and when. In short polling the client asks at fixed intervals; in long
polling it asks and the server waits before answering; with server-sent events one response never ends; with WebSocket
the HTTP connection becomes a channel in both directions. The definition states each by its rules, so that the
proposition can compute with them.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-real-time-delivery}
#### Methods of real-time delivery

Let a server generate **events** for a client at times $e_1 < e_2 < \cdots$ and let $N_e(T)$ be the number of events in
$(0, T]$. A **method of real-time delivery** is a protocol by which the events reach the client; the **delay** of an event
is the time from its generation to its receipt.

1. (**Short polling**) The client sends a request every $\Delta$ seconds; the server answers each at once with the
   events generated and not yet delivered, possibly none [@rfc6202, Sec. 2.1].
2. (**Long polling**) The client sends a request; the server holds it until it has an undelivered event, and then
   answers with all undelivered events, or until it has held it for a **timeout** $\theta$, and then answers with none;
   on receiving any answer the client sends the next request [@rfc6202, Sec. 2.1].
3. (**Server-sent events**) The client sends one HTTP request; the server answers with a response of type
   `text/event-stream` that it never completes, writing each event into it as a block of `data:` lines ended by an empty
   line, optionally with an `id:` line; if the connection breaks, the client reconnects and sends the last identifier
   it received in a `Last-Event-ID` field [@whatwgHTML, Secs. 9.2.1, 9.2.4 and 9.2.5].
4. (**WebSocket**) The client sends an HTTP request with `Upgrade: websocket`; the server answers `101 Switching
   Protocols`, and from then on both sides send framed messages over the same TCP connection, in either direction and at
   any time, including Ping and Pong frames that test whether the other side is still there [@rfc6455, Secs. 1.3, 5.2
   and 5.5].

A **heartbeat** is a message sent every $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$ seconds only to show that the sender is alive; the receiver declares the
sender gone if no heartbeat arrives for a **timeout** longer than $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$.
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Liu's three uses show what the methods are for. In each, the server learns something the client is waiting for.

::: {#exm-rt-liu-uses}
#### Three uses

"While other users send messages in a chat system, the end-user needs to see the new messages in real-time. In a
notification system, the end-users need to receive a notification whenever a relevant event happens. In a time-series
dashboard like a stock graph, users want to see the updated graph as new price feeds come in"
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Use Case"]. The events are messages, notifications and prices; their rates differ
by orders of magnitude, from a few a day to several a second.
:::

Xu separates the two directions of a chat. Only the receiver's side needs one of the methods.

::: {#exm-rt-xu-receiver}
#### Sender and receiver

On the sender's side "it uses the time-tested HTTP protocol", with keep-alive to avoid repeated handshakes; "however, the
receiver side is a bit more complicated. Since HTTP is client-initiated, it is not trivial to send messages from the
server" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 12, Step 2]. Sending a message is an ordinary request; receiving one is the
problem of the definition.
:::

RFC 6202 defines short polling by its cost. The cost depends on the delay the client will accept.

::: {#exm-rt-short-polling}
#### Short polling

"A client sends regular requests to the server and each request attempts to 'pull' any available events or data. If there
are no events or data available, the server returns an empty response"; the resources consumed "strongly depend on the
acceptable latency in the delivery of updates" [@rfc6202, Sec. 2.1]. Liu is blunter: "you may be invoking many requests
with no update and overloading the servers unnecessarily" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Short Poll"].
:::

Long polling changes one rule: the server waits. The standard's life cycle has four steps.

::: {#exm-rt-long-polling}
#### The life cycle of a long poll

"1. The client makes an initial request and then waits for a response. 2. The server defers its response until an update
is available or until a particular status or timeout has occurred. 3. When an update is available, the server sends a
complete response to the client. 4. The client typically sends a new long poll request" [@rfc6202, Sec. 2.1]. At any time
the server holds one request per client, to which it "replies when new information is available".
:::

Server-sent events are a single long response. The HTML standard's first example shows the format.

::: {#exm-rt-sse-format}
#### An event stream

The server sends, with the type `text/event-stream`, the lines `data: This is the first message.`, an empty line,
`data: This is the second message, it`, `data: has two lines.`, an empty line, and so on; a stream can also name event
types with `event: add` and `event: remove` [@whatwgHTML, Sec. 9.2.1]. Each empty line ends one event. In the browser,
`new EventSource('updates.cgi')` opens the stream and calls a handler for every event.
:::

The WebSocket handshake is an HTTP request. RFC 6455 gives an example of both messages.

::: {#exm-rt-websocket-handshake}
#### The opening handshake

The client sends `GET /chat HTTP/1.1` with `Host: server.example.com`, `Upgrade: websocket`, `Connection: Upgrade`,
`Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==` and `Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13`; the server answers `HTTP/1.1 101 Switching
Protocols` with `Sec-WebSocket-Accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=` [@rfc6455, Sec. 1.3]. The handshake "is intended to be
compatible with HTTP-based server-side software and intermediaries", which is why it works "over HTTP ports 80 and 443"
[@rfc6455, Secs. 1.1 and 1.3].
:::

After the handshake, messages are framed with very little overhead. The frame header's size depends on the payload's.

::: {#exm-rt-frame-overhead}
#### A small frame

A frame's payload length takes "7 bits, 7+16 bits, or 7+64 bits": a payload of up to $125$ bytes needs one length byte,
so with the byte of flags and opcode the header is $2$ bytes, and a frame from the client adds a $4$-byte masking key
[@rfc6455, Sec. 5.2]. A $100$-byte chat message from the server costs $102$ bytes, against the hundreds of bytes of HTTP
header fields of every long-poll response (@exr-net-header-overhead).
:::

A heartbeat turns silence into information. Xu uses it for the online indicator of a chat.

::: {#exm-rt-xu-heartbeat}
#### Presence by heartbeat

"Periodically, an online client sends a heartbeat event to presence servers. If presence servers receive a heartbeat
event within a certain time, say x seconds from the client, a user is considered as online"; in Xu's figure "the client
sends a heartbeat event to the server every 5 seconds", and the user is marked offline after "x = 30 seconds"
[@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 12, "User disconnection"]. In the definition's terms $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}} = 5\,\mathrm{s}$ and the timeout
is $30\,\mathrm{s}$, so a brief tunnel does not flip the indicator.
:::

Persistent connections change how a balancer works. Liu's design hands out connection servers instead of balancing
requests.

::: {#exm-rt-liu-ws-balancer}
#### Balancing WebSocket connections

"For a WebSocket, you need to establish a stateful connection to a physical server with IP and port"; the common approach
"is to have a load balancer that hands out the endpoint of a WebSocket proxy farm", and "when the WebSocket server goes
down, all the clients connected to the WebSocket server need to reconnect. This disconnection can cause a thundering
herd onto other servers" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "WebSocket Load Balancer"]. The connection servers are
stateful in the sense of @def-stateless-service.
:::

Held connections cost memory, not processing. Xu's estimate shows how little.

::: {#exm-rt-connection-memory}
#### Memory per connection

"At 1M concurrent users, assuming each user connection needs 10K of memory on the server (this is a very rough figure
and very dependent on the language choice), it only needs about 10GB of memory to hold all the connections on one box"
[@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 12, "Scalability"]. A long poll holds a connection and a request for every client too;
RFC 6202 warns that "the resources allocated to HTTP requests can be significant" [@rfc6202, Sec. 2.2].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise chooses a method for four products. It uses Liu's advice to prefer SSE for one-way traffic and
WebSocket otherwise.

::: {#exr-rt-choose}
#### Choosing a method

Choose a method of @def-real-time-delivery for (1) a stock ticker in a browser, (2) a chat in a mobile app, (3) an admin
dashboard refreshed once a minute, used by ten people, and (4) a notification of a finished upload, about once a day per
user, in a client that cannot hold connections open.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

(1) Server-sent events: traffic is one-way, frequent, and SSE "uses the traditional HTTP", so it is "less work to get SSE
working" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "How to Pick a Protocol"]. (2) WebSocket: messages go both ways, and the
same connection can carry sends and receipts, as in Xu's design. (3) Short polling once a minute: ten clients make ten
requests a minute, and no connection infrastructure is needed. (4) Long polling or short polling on the app's next
request; the push services of the phone platforms are the usual answer, outside this section.

## Python

The choice as a rule on two properties: direction and rate.

```{.python .run}
def choose(two_way, events_per_hour, many_clients, can_hold_connection=True):
    if not can_hold_connection:
        return "long polling (or polling)"
    if two_way:
        return "WebSocket"
    if events_per_hour >= 60 and many_clients:
        return "server-sent events"
    return "short polling"
for name, args in (("stock ticker", (False, 3600, True)), ("mobile chat", (True, 20, True)),
                   ("admin dashboard", (False, 60, False)), ("upload done", (False, 0.04, True, False))):
    print(f"{name:15s}: {choose(*args)}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
stock ticker   : server-sent events
mobile chat    : WebSocket
admin dashboard: short polling
upload done    : long polling (or polling)
```
::::
:::

The second exercise parses an event stream by the rules of the HTML standard. A client must split the stream into events
exactly as the server meant.

::: {#exr-rt-sse-parse}
#### Parsing an event stream

Write a parser that splits a `text/event-stream` into events: a line `field: value` sets a field (`data` lines are joined
with newlines, `event` sets the type, `id` the last event identifier), a line starting with a colon is a comment, and an
empty line dispatches the event if it has data [@whatwgHTML, Sec. 9.2.6]. Apply it to a stream with two events, a
comment, a two-line message and identifiers.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The parser keeps a buffer for the data, the type and the last identifier, appends each `data` value with a newline,
ignores comments, and on an empty line emits (type, data without the final newline, last identifier) and clears the data
and type. The last identifier persists across events, which is what the client sends in `Last-Event-ID` after a
reconnection.

## Python

The parser and the stream.

```{.python .run}
def parse(stream):
    events, data, etype, last_id = [], [], "message", ""
    for line in stream.split("\n"):
        if line == "":
            if data:
                events.append((etype, "\n".join(data), last_id))
            data, etype = [], "message"
            continue
        if line.startswith(":"):
            continue
        field, _, value = line.partition(":")
        value = value[1:] if value.startswith(" ") else value
        if field == "data":
            data.append(value)
        elif field == "event":
            etype = value
        elif field == "id":
            last_id = value
    return events
stream = ("id: 1\ndata: first message\n\n: keep-alive comment\n\nevent: like\nid: 2\ndata: photo 123\n\n"
          "data: second message, it\ndata: has two lines.\n\n")
for e in parse(stream):
    print(e)
```

```{.text .run-output}
('message', 'first message', '1')
('like', 'photo 123', '2')
('message', 'second message, it\nhas two lines.', '2')
```
::::
:::

The third exercise computes the server's answer to a WebSocket handshake. The key and the answer of @exm-rt-websocket-handshake
must agree.

::: {#exr-rt-accept-key}
#### The accept value

The server "would concatenate the string '258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11'" to the client's key, hash the result with
SHA-1 and encode the hash in base64 [@rfc6455, Sec. 1.3]. Compute the accept value for the key `dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==`
and check it against the standard's example. What does the exchange prove to the client?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The computation gives `s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=`, the value in the standard. It proves that the server read the
handshake and understood it as a WebSocket handshake, since an ordinary HTTP server would not produce this value; it is
not authentication, which the connection gets from TLS and from the application.

## Python

The accept value.

```{.python .run}
import base64, hashlib
key = "dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ=="
accept = base64.b64encode(hashlib.sha1((key + "258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11").encode()).digest()).decode()
print(accept, accept == "s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=")
```

```{.text .run-output}
s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo= True
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise writes the size rule of the frame header as a function. It extends @exm-rt-frame-overhead to every
payload size.

::: {#exr-rt-frame-header}
#### The size of a frame header

From the rule that the length takes 7 bits for payloads up to $125$ bytes, 7+16 bits up to $65\,535$ and 7+64 bits beyond,
and a $4$-byte masking key on frames from the client [@rfc6455, Sec. 5.2], give the header size for payloads of $10$,
$125$, $126$, $65\,535$, $65\,536$ and $10^6$ bytes from each side, and the overhead in percent.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Server to client: $2$ bytes up to $125$, $4$ up to $65\,535$ and $10$ beyond; client to server $4$ more. For a $10$-byte
message the overhead is $20\%$ from the server and $60\%$ from the client; for $65\,536$ bytes it is $0.02\%$. The frames'
overhead matters only for tiny messages, unlike HTTP's.

## Python

The header sizes.

```{.python .run}
def header(payload, from_client):
    length = 1 if payload <= 125 else 3 if payload <= 65535 else 9
    return 1 + length + (4 if from_client else 0)
for n in (10, 125, 126, 65535, 65536, 10**6):
    s, c = header(n, False), header(n, True)
    print(f"{n:>8} bytes: server {s:2d} ({s / n:.2%}), client {c:2d} ({c / n:.2%})")
```

```{.text .run-output}
      10 bytes: server  2 (20.00%), client  6 (60.00%)
     125 bytes: server  2 (1.60%), client  6 (4.80%)
     126 bytes: server  4 (3.17%), client  8 (6.35%)
   65535 bytes: server  4 (0.01%), client  8 (0.01%)
   65536 bytes: server 10 (0.02%), client 14 (0.02%)
 1000000 bytes: server 10 (0.00%), client 14 (0.00%)
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise checks Liu's description of server-sent events. It disagrees with the standards.

::: {#exr-rt-liu-sse}
#### Who keeps the connection open?

Liu writes that with SSE "the server keeps the connection open, but the client doesn't keep the connection open"
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Server-Sent Event"]. Compare with item 3 of the definition and with RFC 6202's
definition of HTTP streaming. What is true in Liu's sentence?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A TCP connection is open at both ends or at neither. With SSE the client holds an open request whose response never
ends: "The server keeps a request open indefinitely; that is, it never terminates the request or closes the connection,
even after it pushes data to the client" [@rfc6202, Sec. 1], and the browser reconnects when the connection breaks
[@whatwgHTML, Sec. 9.2.4]. What is true is that the client sends nothing on the connection after its request: the
traffic is one-way.

## Python

A trace of who sends what on one SSE connection.

```{.python .run}
trace = [("client", "GET /updates (Accept: text/event-stream)"), ("server", "200 OK, Content-Type: text/event-stream"),
         ("server", "data: price 101.2"), ("server", "data: price 101.5"), ("server", "data: price 101.1")]
print("messages from the client after the request:", sum(1 for who, _ in trace[1:] if who == "client"))
print("connection open at the client while events arrive:", True)
```

```{.text .run-output}
messages from the client after the request: 0
connection open at the client while events arrive: True
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise checks Tan's claim that WebSocket needs no backend. The handshake of item 4 says otherwise.

::: {#exr-rt-tan-p2p}
#### Peer to peer?

Tan writes that "WebSocket allows p2p communication, so no backend is required" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 6.7.5,
p. 142]. Using the opening handshake of RFC 6455, explain why two browsers cannot open a WebSocket connection to each
other, and what a chat between them needs instead.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The opening handshake is an HTTP request from a client to a server that listens for it [@rfc6455, Sec. 1.3]; a browser
runs clients only and cannot accept the request. Two browsers therefore each open a WebSocket to a server, which relays
the messages: exactly the chat service of Xu's design. Tan's other statement in the same section, that WebSocket is
stateful and that "a request must be handled by the host that contains the relevant state/connection", is right, and is
the reason for the connection servers of @exm-rt-liu-ws-balancer.

## Python

The relay as the only path between two clients.

```{.python .run}
accepts_handshakes = {"browser A": False, "browser B": False, "chat server": True}
links = [(c, s) for c in ("browser A", "browser B") for s, ok in accepts_handshakes.items() if ok and s != c]
print("possible connections:", links)
print("path from A to B:", ["browser A", "chat server", "browser B"])
```

```{.text .run-output}
possible connections: [('browser A', 'chat server'), ('browser B', 'chat server')]
path from A to B: ['browser A', 'chat server', 'browser B']
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise sizes the connection servers' memory. It uses Xu's figure of $10\,\mathrm{kB}$ per connection.

::: {#exr-rt-memory}
#### Memory for the connections

A third of the photo service's $10^8$ daily users are connected at the peak, each by one WebSocket. With $10\,\mathrm{kB}$
per connection [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 12, "Scalability"], how much memory do the connections take, and how many
servers with $64\,\mathrm{GB}$, of which half may be used for connections?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$3.33 \times 10^7 \times 10^4 = 3.33 \times 10^{11}$ bytes, $333\,\mathrm{GB}$. With $32\,\mathrm{GB}$ per server for
connections, $11$ servers. Memory is not the limit here; @exr-load-chat used Liu's limit of $10^6$ connections per server,
which gives $34$.

## Python

The memory and the two counts.

```{.python .run}
from math import ceil
connected = 1e8 / 3
memory = connected * 10e3
print(f"memory {memory / 1e9:.0f} GB; servers by memory {ceil(memory / 32e9)}; by 10^6 connections each {ceil(connected / 1e6)}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
memory 333 GB; servers by memory 11; by 10^6 connections each 34
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise asks what a layer-4 balancer does with connections that last hours. The rebalancing of
@exr-scale-rebalance applies.

::: {#exr-rt-ws-rebalance}
#### Adding a connection server

A pool of $34$ connection servers holds $3.3 \times 10^7$ WebSockets, each open for an exponentially distributed time of mean
$4$ hours, and a new server is added; new connections are spread evenly over all $35$. How long until the new server holds
half its fair share? Why is closing some connections on the old servers deliberately an option for WebSockets and not for
the sticky sessions of @def-stateless-service?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

As in @exr-scale-rebalance the new server's share of its fair share after time $t$ is $1 - e^{-t/4\,\mathrm{h}}$, one half
after $4\log 2 = 2.8$ hours. A WebSocket client reconnects on its own when its connection closes, and its state (the
subscriptions) is rebuilt from the shared store, so closing a fraction of the old connections, a few at a time, moves them
without losing anything; a sticky session's state is lost with its server.

## Python

The time to half the fair share.

```{.python .run}
from math import log
mean_hours = 4
print(f"half the fair share after {mean_hours * log(2):.1f} hours; 90% after {mean_hours * log(10):.1f} hours")
```

```{.text .run-output}
half the fair share after 2.8 hours; 90% after 9.2 hours
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise sizes the routing table that a push design needs. Liu calls it the mapping from users to WebSocket
servers.

::: {#exr-rt-routing-table}
#### Which server holds the user?

To deliver an event to a user, a service looks up the connection server that holds the user's connection, in a store that
Liu describes as "a mapping store from a user attribute to all the WebSocket servers" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020,
Ch. 5, "WebSocket Load Balancer"]. With $3.3 \times 10^7$ connected users, $40$ bytes per entry, connections opened and
closed at an average of one per user per hour, and events at $2 \times 10^4$ per second, give the size of the table and its
write and read rates.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The table holds $3.3 \times 10^7 \times 40 = 1.3\,\mathrm{GB}$. Each opening and closing writes it: about $2 \times 3.3
\times 10^7/3600 = 1.8 \times 10^4$ writes per second. Each event reads it: $2 \times 10^4$ reads per second. A replicated
in-memory store serves both.

## Python

The three numbers.

```{.python .run}
users, entry, events = 3.3e7, 40, 2e4
print(f"size {users * entry / 1e9:.2f} GB; writes {2 * users / 3600:,.0f}/s; reads {events:,.0f}/s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
size 1.32 GB; writes 18,333/s; reads 20,000/s
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise implements liveness by Ping and Pong. It compares the detection time with the number of messages.

::: {#exr-rt-ping-pong}
#### Detecting a dead peer

A server sends a Ping every $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$ seconds and declares the client dead when no Pong has arrived for $3\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$, the client
answering each Ping at once [@rfc6455, Sec. 5.5.2]. For a client that disappears at a uniformly random time, simulate the
detection delay for $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}} = 10\,\mathrm{s}$ and give its range and mean, and the Pings per day per connection.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The last Pong arrives at the last Ping before the disappearance, at a time $U$ uniform on $(0, \Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}]$ before it (neglecting
the network); the client is declared dead $3\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$ after that Pong, so the delay is $3\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}} - U$, between $2\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$ and $3\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$, with mean
$2.5\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}} = 25\,\mathrm{s}$. Each connection costs $8640$ Pings and Pongs a day.

## Python

A seeded simulation of the delay.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
h = 10.0
death = rng.uniform(1000, 2000, 100_000)
last_pong = np.floor(death / h) * h                 # pings at multiples of h, answered at once
delay = last_pong + 3 * h - death
print(f"delay between {delay.min():.1f} and {delay.max():.1f} s, mean {delay.mean():.2f} s; pings per day {86400 / h:.0f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
delay between 20.0 and 30.0 s, mean 25.02 s; pings per day 8640
```
::::
:::
::::

### Delay and cost of polling and push

The methods trade delay against requests. Short polling buys a shorter delay only with more requests; long polling and
push cut both, at the price of held connections. The proposition makes each trade-off exact under a simple model of the
network: the connection is already open, every message takes $\mathrm{RTT}/2$, nothing is lost and nothing takes time
to process. RFC 6202 states part (b) in words: "while the average latency of long polling is close to one network
transit, the maximal latency is over three network transits (long poll response, next long poll request, long poll
response)" [@rfc6202, Sec. 2.2].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-rt-polling}
#### Delay and requests of real-time delivery

Under the model above, with events at times $e_1 < e_2 < \cdots$ and $N_e(T)$ of them in $(0, T]$, let an event generated
exactly when a request arrives be included in its answer.

(a) (**Short polling**) With requests sent at times $0, \Delta, 2\Delta, \dots$, the client sends $\lfloor T/\Delta\rfloor
+ 1$ requests in $[0, T]$ whatever the events, and every event generated after $\mathrm{RTT}/2$ has a delay $D$ with
$\mathrm{RTT}/2 \leq D < \Delta + \mathrm{RTT}/2$. If the time from the event to the arrival of the next request is
uniformly distributed on $[0, \Delta)$, then $\mathbb E[D] = \Delta/2 + \mathrm{RTT}/2$.

(b) (**Long polling**) With timeout $\theta > 0$, every event generated after $\mathrm{RTT}/2$ has a delay $D$ with
$\mathrm{RTT}/2 \leq D \leq \tfrac32\mathrm{RTT}$, and the client sends at most $N_e(T) + T/\theta + 1$ requests in $[0,
T]$.

(c) (**Push**) Over an open server-sent-event stream or WebSocket on which the server writes each event when it is
generated, every event has delay exactly $\mathrm{RTT}/2$, and the server sends $N_e(T)$ messages in $(0, T]$ and the
client none; heartbeats every $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$ add $\lfloor T/\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}\rfloor$ messages.
:::

::::

*Proof.* (a) The requests are sent at $j\Delta$ for the integers $0 \leq j \leq T/\Delta$, whatever happens. Request $j$
arrives at $a_j = j\Delta + \mathrm{RTT}/2$ and its answer at $a_j + \mathrm{RTT}/2$. An event at $e > \mathrm{RTT}/2$ is
in the answer to the first request with $a_j \geq e$, since earlier requests arrived before it and later ones find it
delivered. With $j$ that index, $a_j \geq e > a_{j-1} = a_j - \Delta$, so the waiting time $W = a_j - e$ lies in $[0,
\Delta)$, and $D = W + \mathrm{RTT}/2$ lies in $[\mathrm{RTT}/2, \Delta + \mathrm{RTT}/2)$. If $W$ is uniform on $[0,
\Delta)$, then $\mathbb E[D] = \Delta/2 + \mathrm{RTT}/2$ by linearity.

(b) At every moment after the first request has arrived, either the server holds a request or an answer and the next
request are in transit: an answer sent at time $s$ reaches the client at $s + \mathrm{RTT}/2$, and the next request, sent
at once, reaches the server at $s + \mathrm{RTT}$. Let an event be generated at $e > \mathrm{RTT}/2$. If the server holds
a request at $e$, it answers at once and $D = \mathrm{RTT}/2$. Otherwise the last answer was sent at some $s$ with $s \leq
e < s + \mathrm{RTT}$; the next request arrives at $s + \mathrm{RTT}$, finds the event undelivered and is answered at
once, so the event arrives at $s + \tfrac32\mathrm{RTT} \leq e + \tfrac32\mathrm{RTT}$, and it cannot arrive before $e +
\mathrm{RTT}/2$, since every answer travels for $\mathrm{RTT}/2$ after it is sent. For the count, the client has at most
one request outstanding at a time, so the requests it sent in $[0, T]$ are those answered by time $T$ and at most one
more. An answer either carries at least one event, generated before it was sent and never delivered again, or is a timeout
after the server held its request for $\theta$. There are at most $N_e(T)$ answers of the first kind. The holding periods
of different requests are disjoint subintervals of $[0, T]$, so there are at most $T/\theta$ answers of the second kind.

(c) Each event is written at its generation and arrives $\mathrm{RTT}/2$ later; one message per event and one per
heartbeat are sent, and the client sends nothing after the stream or connection is open. $\square$

Part (a) contains the trade-off of short polling in one line: the request rate $1/\Delta$ times the worst extra delay
$\Delta$ is one, so halving the delay doubles the requests, for every client and whether or not anything happens. Part (b)
removes the dependence on $\Delta$: requests follow the events, plus a slow trickle of timeouts, and the delay is at most
three transits. Part (c) removes the requests altogether, at the cost of a connection held open for as long as the client
wants events.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Short polling's cost is paid by every client. Liu's warning is part (a) with numbers.

::: {#exm-poll-liu-cost}
#### A million clients polling

A million connected clients polling every $\Delta = 5\,\mathrm{s}$ send $2 \times 10^5$ requests per second by part (a),
whether or not any event happens. With an average delay of $2.5\,\mathrm{s}$ plus half a round trip, this is the "many
requests with no update" of Liu [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Short Poll"].
:::

A staleness requirement fixes the polling period. The previous chapter stated one for the photo feed.

::: {#exm-poll-staleness}
#### The period for a staleness target

@exm-req-staleness asks that a new photo appear in a follower's feed within $5\,\mathrm{s}$ with probability $0.99$. With
uniform waiting as in part (a) and $\mathrm{RTT} = 100\,\mathrm{ms}$, $\mathbb P(D \leq 5) = (5 - 0.05)/\Delta \geq
0.99$ needs $\Delta \leq 5.0\,\mathrm{s}$. Ten million open feeds would then poll at $2 \times 10^6$ requests per second,
more than ten times the feed's peak.
:::

Most polls of a quiet client are empty. The chat of the previous chapter is quiet by this measure.

::: {#exm-poll-empty}
#### Empty answers

A chat user receives $40$ messages a day (@exr-load-chat). Polling every $5\,\mathrm{s}$ makes $17\,280$ requests a day by
part (a), of which at most $40$ carry a message: at least $99.8\%$ of the answers are empty.
:::

Long polling makes the count follow the events. The timeout adds a small floor.

::: {#exm-poll-long-count}
#### The same user with long polls

With long polls and $\theta = 30\,\mathrm{s}$, the user makes at most $40 + 2880 + 1 = 2921$ requests a day by part (b),
six times fewer than with polling every $5\,\mathrm{s}$, and receives each message within $1.5$ round trips instead of up
to $5\,\mathrm{s}$. Xu's remark that long polling "still makes periodic connections after timeouts" if "a user does not
chat much" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 12, "Long polling"] is the term $T/\theta$.
:::

RFC 6202's "three network transits" is the bound of part (b). The worst case is an event just after an answer.

::: {#exm-poll-three-transits}
#### The worst case of long polling

If an event occurs just after the server has answered the previous long poll, it waits for that answer to reach the
client ($\mathrm{RTT}/2$), for the next request to come back ($\mathrm{RTT}/2$) and for its own answer
($\mathrm{RTT}/2$): $\tfrac32\mathrm{RTT}$, the "long poll response, next long poll request, long poll response" of
[@rfc6202, Sec. 2.2]. With $\mathrm{RTT} = 100\,\mathrm{ms}$ that is $150\,\mathrm{ms}$.
:::

Push makes heartbeats the dominant traffic of a quiet client. Xu's presence heartbeat is an example.

::: {#exm-poll-heartbeats}
#### Heartbeats outnumber messages

With a WebSocket, the chat user's $40$ messages arrive after half a round trip each, by part (c). Xu's heartbeat every
$5\,\mathrm{s}$ [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 12, "User disconnection"] adds $17\,280$ messages a day, as many as
polling every $5\,\mathrm{s}$; but each is a frame of a few bytes (@exm-rt-frame-overhead) rather than an HTTP request and
response.
:::

The proof of part (b) can be followed in a simulation. The run sends random events to a long-polling client and records
the delays.

::: {#exm-poll-simulation}
#### A simulated long poll

With $\mathrm{RTT} = 100\,\mathrm{ms}$, $\theta = 30\,\mathrm{s}$ and $2000$ events at random times over a day of
simulated time, every delay lies between $50$ and $150\,\mathrm{ms}$, and the number of requests stays below $N_e(T) +
T/\theta + 1$.

```{.python .run}
import simpy, numpy as np
RTT, THETA, T = 0.1, 30.0, 86400.0
rng = np.random.default_rng(17)
events = np.sort(rng.uniform(1, T - 1, 2000))
env = simpy.Environment()
pending, delays, requests = [], [], [0]
arrived = simpy.Store(env)                          # requests arriving at the server
def generator():
    for e in events:
        yield env.timeout(e - env.now)
        pending.append(e)
        if waiting:
            waiting.pop().succeed()
waiting = []
def server():
    while True:
        yield arrived.get()
        if not pending:
            wake = env.event(); waiting.append(wake)
            yield wake | env.timeout(THETA)
            if wake in waiting:
                waiting.remove(wake)
        batch = pending[:]; pending.clear()
        env.process(answer(batch))
def answer(batch):
    yield env.timeout(RTT / 2)                      # the answer travels to the client
    delays.extend(env.now - e for e in batch)
    env.process(request())
def request():
    requests[0] += 1
    yield env.timeout(RTT / 2)
    arrived.put(1)
env.process(generator()); env.process(server()); env.process(request())
env.run(until=T)
d = np.array(delays) * 1000
print(f"events delivered {len(d)}, delay between {d.min():.0f} and {d.max():.0f} ms")
print(f"requests {requests[0]}, bound {len(events) + T / THETA + 1:.0f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
events delivered 2000, delay between 50 and 143 ms
requests 3979, bound 4881
```
:::

Long polling degrades gracefully under load. RFC 6202 explains why.

::: {#exm-poll-batching}
#### Batching under load

"If multiple messages are queued for a client, they might be delivered in a batch within a single long poll response.
This can significantly reduce the per-message overhead" [@rfc6202, Sec. 2.2]. In part (b) an answer may carry many events,
so the count $N_e(T)$ is an upper bound on the answers with events: when events arrive faster than one per round trip,
the requests per event fall below one.
:::

Long polling and push hold resources for every client. The number of open requests is the number of clients.

::: {#exm-poll-held-requests}
#### What is held

At any time after its first request a long-polling client has a request held at the server or in transit (the proof of
part (b)): for $10^6$ clients, about $10^6$ held requests and connections. RFC 6202 notes that "the HTTP long polling
mechanism requires that for each client both a TCP/IP connection and an HTTP request are held open"
[@rfc6202, Sec. 2.2]. Push holds the connection without the request.
:::

The three methods can be compared on one client's day. The run below tabulates parts (a) to (c).

::: {#exm-poll-comparison}
#### One client's day

For a client with $N_e = 40$ events in a day, $\mathrm{RTT} = 100\,\mathrm{ms}$, short polls every $5\,\mathrm{s}$, long
polls with $\theta = 30\,\mathrm{s}$, and push with heartbeats every $30\,\mathrm{s}$:

```{.python .run}
day, events, rtt = 86400, 40, 0.1
rows = [("short polling, 5 s", day // 5 + 1, f"< {5 + rtt / 2:.2f} s, mean {2.5 + rtt / 2:.2f} s"),
        ("long polling, 30 s", events + day // 30 + 1, f"<= {1.5 * rtt:.2f} s"),
        ("push, heartbeat 30 s", events + day // 30, f"= {rtt / 2:.2f} s")]
for name, messages, delay in rows:
    print(f"{name:21s}: at most {messages:6d} requests or messages a day, delay {delay}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
short polling, 5 s   : at most  17281 requests or messages a day, delay < 5.05 s, mean 2.55 s
long polling, 30 s   : at most   2921 requests or messages a day, delay <= 0.15 s
push, heartbeat 30 s : at most   2920 requests or messages a day, delay = 0.05 s
```
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise tabulates part (a). It shows the product of the request rate and the delay.

::: {#exr-poll-table}
#### The polling table

For $\Delta = 1, 5, 30\,\mathrm{s}$ and $\mathrm{RTT} = 100\,\mathrm{ms}$, give the requests per hour, the worst and the mean
delay of short polling, and the product of the request rate and the worst extra delay $\Delta$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

By part (a): $3600$, $720$ and $120$ requests per hour; worst delays just under $1.05$, $5.05$ and $30.05\,\mathrm{s}$;
means $0.55$, $2.55$ and $15.05\,\mathrm{s}$. The product of the rate $1/\Delta$ and $\Delta$ is one in every row.

## Python

The table.

```{.python .run}
rtt = 0.1
for delta in (1, 5, 30):
    print(f"Delta = {delta:2d} s: {3600 // delta:4d} requests/hour, worst < {delta + rtt / 2:.2f} s, "
          f"mean {delta / 2 + rtt / 2:.2f} s, rate x Delta = {(1 / delta) * delta:.0f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
Delta =  1 s: 3600 requests/hour, worst < 1.05 s, mean 0.55 s, rate x Delta = 1
Delta =  5 s:  720 requests/hour, worst < 5.05 s, mean 2.55 s, rate x Delta = 1
Delta = 30 s:  120 requests/hour, worst < 30.05 s, mean 15.05 s, rate x Delta = 1
```
::::
:::

The second exercise justifies the assumption of part (a) about uniform waiting. It holds when events do not know the
polling schedule.

::: {#exr-poll-uniform-phase}
#### Why the waiting is uniform

Let an event's time be $e = m\Delta + \mathrm{RTT}/2 - V$ with an integer $m$ and $V$ uniform on $(0, \Delta]$, for
example because the client started polling at a time unrelated to the event. Prove that the waiting time $W$ of the proof is
then uniform on $[0, \Delta)$, so that $\mathbb E[D] = \Delta/2 + \mathrm{RTT}/2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Write $a_j = j\Delta + \mathrm{RTT}/2$ for the arrival of request $j$, so that $e = a_m - V$. If $V < \Delta$, then
$a_{m-1} = a_m - \Delta < e < a_m$, the first arrival at or after $e$ is $a_m$, and $W = a_m - e = V$. If $V = \Delta$,
then $e = a_{m-1}$ and $W = 0$. So $W = V$ except on the event $\{V = \Delta\}$, which has probability zero; hence $W$ is
uniform on $[0, \Delta)$, $\mathbb E[W] = \Delta/2$, and $\mathbb E[D] = \mathbb E[W] + \mathrm{RTT}/2$.

## Python

The waiting time computed from the rule of the proof for seeded uniform $V$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
delta, rtt = 5.0, 0.1
V = rng.uniform(0, delta, 200_000)
e = 40 * delta + rtt / 2 - V
j = np.ceil((e - rtt / 2) / delta)                 # first request arriving at or after e
W = j * delta + rtt / 2 - e
print(f"W in [{W.min():.4f}, {W.max():.4f}], mean {W.mean():.4f} (Delta/2 = {delta / 2})")
```

```{.text .run-output}
W in [0.0000, 5.0000], mean 2.5014 (Delta/2 = 2.5)
```
::::
:::

The third exercise simulates short polling and draws its delay distribution as a histogram in text. The distribution
should be uniform.

::: {#exr-poll-simulate-short}
#### The delay of short polling

Simulate short polling with $\Delta = 5\,\mathrm{s}$ and $\mathrm{RTT} = 100\,\mathrm{ms}$ for $10^5$ events at random
times, and print the fraction of delays in each second. Compare with part (a).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The delays fill $[0.05, 5.05)$, about a fifth in each of the first five seconds and the remaining $1\%$ in $[5, 5.05)$, as
part (a) with uniform waiting predicts, and their mean is close to $2.55\,\mathrm{s}$.

## Python

Seeded event times and the rule of the proof.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(14)
delta, rtt = 5.0, 0.1
e = rng.uniform(1, 10_000, 100_000)
j = np.ceil((e - rtt / 2) / delta)
D = j * delta + rtt - e
counts, _ = np.histogram(D, bins=[0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])
print("fraction per second:", np.round(counts / len(D), 3), f"| mean {D.mean():.3f} s, max {D.max():.3f} s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
fraction per second: [0.189 0.199 0.198 0.202 0.202 0.01 ] | mean 2.561 s, max 5.050 s
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise chooses the polling period for a percentile target. It inverts part (a).

::: {#exr-poll-choose-period}
#### A period for a percentile

A dashboard requires $t_{0.99} \leq 2\,\mathrm{s}$ for the delay of its updates, with $\mathrm{RTT} = 100\,\mathrm{ms}$ and
uniform waiting. Give the largest $\Delta$ and the load of $10^5$ dashboards, and compare with long polling, whose delay
is at most $0.15\,\mathrm{s}$ by part (b), for $1$ update per minute per dashboard and $\theta = 60\,\mathrm{s}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$\mathbb P(D \leq t) = (t - 0.05)/\Delta$ for $t$ in the range, so $t_{0.99} = 0.05 + 0.99\Delta \leq 2$ gives $\Delta \leq
1.97\,\mathrm{s}$, and $10^5$ dashboards poll at $5.1 \times 10^4$ requests per second. Long polling makes at most $1/60 +
1/60$ requests per second per dashboard, $3.3 \times 10^3$ in all, fifteen times fewer, with a delay below
$0.15\,\mathrm{s}$.

## Python

The period and the two loads.

```{.python .run}
rtt, target, clients = 0.1, 2.0, 1e5
delta = (target - rtt / 2) / 0.99
print(f"Delta <= {delta:.3f} s; short polling {clients / delta:,.0f}/s; long polling <= {clients * (1 / 60 + 1 / 60):,.0f}/s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
Delta <= 1.970 s; short polling 50,769/s; long polling <= 3,333/s
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise shows that the bound of part (b) cannot be improved. An event can arrive at the worst moment.

::: {#exr-poll-sharp}
#### The bound is attained

Prove that for every $\epsilon > 0$ there is an event whose long-poll delay exceeds $\tfrac32\mathrm{RTT} - \epsilon$, so
that the upper bound of part (b) is the best possible under the model.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Let the server send an answer at time $s$ (an event answer or a timeout). Take an event at $e = s + \eta$ with $0 < \eta <
\min(\epsilon, \mathrm{RTT})$ and no other event in $(s, e)$. No request is held during $(s, s + \mathrm{RTT})$, so by the
proof the event is answered when the next request arrives, at $s + \mathrm{RTT}$, and received at $s + \tfrac32
\mathrm{RTT}$; its delay is $\tfrac32\mathrm{RTT} - \eta > \tfrac32\mathrm{RTT} - \epsilon$.

## Python

The delay of an event $\eta$ after an answer, for decreasing $\eta$.

```{.python .run}
rtt = 0.1
for eta in (0.05, 0.01, 0.001):
    s = 10.0
    delivered = s + rtt + rtt / 2                   # next request arrives at s + RTT, answer takes RTT/2
    print(f"eta = {eta}: delay {(delivered - (s + eta)) * 1000:.0f} ms (bound {1.5 * rtt * 1000:.0f} ms)")
```

```{.text .run-output}
eta = 0.05: delay 100 ms (bound 150 ms)
eta = 0.01: delay 140 ms (bound 150 ms)
eta = 0.001: delay 149 ms (bound 150 ms)
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise finds when long polling makes more requests than short polling. Busy clients reverse the order.

::: {#exr-poll-break-even}
#### When long polling is busier

A client receives events at an average rate $r_e$ per second, spread so that each long-poll answer carries one event.
Using the bound of part (b), show that long polling makes at most as many requests as short polling with period $\Delta$
when $r_e \leq 1/\Delta - 1/\theta$, and compute the break-even for $\Delta = 5\,\mathrm{s}$ and $\theta = 30\,\mathrm{s}$.
What happens to a stock ticker with ten updates per second?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Per unit time, long polling makes at most $r_e + 1/\theta$ requests (part (b)) and short polling $1/\Delta$ (part (a)),
so the first is at most the second when $r_e \leq 1/\Delta - 1/\theta = 0.2 - 0.033 = 0.167$ events per second. With ten
updates per second each long poll would carry about one event per round trip, up to ten requests per second, fifty
times short polling's; this is the case for push, part (c), or for batching (@exm-poll-batching).

## Python

The break-even and the ticker.

```{.python .run}
delta, theta = 5.0, 30.0
print(f"break-even event rate {1 / delta - 1 / theta:.3f}/s; ticker: long polling up to {10 + 1 / theta:.2f} requests/s "
      f"against {1 / delta:.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
break-even event rate 0.167/s; ticker: long polling up to 10.03 requests/s against 0.20
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise compares the bytes per event. Long polling sends a full HTTP exchange; push a frame.

::: {#exr-poll-bytes}
#### Bytes per event

A long-poll request and answer carry $700$ bytes of headers together, and an event's payload is $100$ bytes; a WebSocket
frame from the server adds $2$ bytes (@exm-rt-frame-overhead), and a heartbeat Ping and Pong cost $12$ bytes. For the
chat user of @exm-poll-long-count, compare the daily bytes of long polling ($\theta = 30\,\mathrm{s}$) and of a WebSocket
with a Ping every $30\,\mathrm{s}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Long polling: at most $2921$ exchanges of $700$ bytes plus $40 \times 100$ bytes of payload, about $2.05\,\mathrm{MB}$ a
day. WebSocket: $40 \times 102$ bytes of messages and $2880 \times 12$ bytes of heartbeats, about $39\,\mathrm{kB}$, fifty
times less. For a quiet client almost all bytes are overhead, and push removes most of it.

## Python

The two totals.

```{.python .run}
events, day, theta = 40, 86400, 30
long_poll = (events + day // theta + 1) * 700 + events * 100
websocket = events * 102 + (day // theta) * 12
print(f"long polling {long_poll / 1e6:.2f} MB/day, WebSocket {websocket / 1e3:.1f} kB/day, ratio {long_poll / websocket:.0f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
long polling 2.05 MB/day, WebSocket 38.6 kB/day, ratio 53
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise studies the presence timeout of @exm-rt-xu-heartbeat. A short timeout flips the indicator when a few
heartbeats are lost.

::: {#exr-poll-presence}
#### Presence by heartbeat

Heartbeats are sent every $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}} = 5\,\mathrm{s}$ and the user is marked offline after a timeout of $x$ seconds without one.
Give the range of the time between a real disconnection and the offline mark, and, if each heartbeat is lost independently
with probability $0.02$, the probability that a connected user is wrongly marked offline at a given heartbeat because the
last $x/\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$ heartbeats were lost, for $x = 10, 15, 30\,\mathrm{s}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The last heartbeat arrives up to $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$ before the disconnection, so the mark comes between $x - \Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$ and $x$ after it: $5$ to
$10$, $10$ to $15$, or $25$ to $30$ seconds. A wrong mark needs $x/\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}}$ consecutive losses: $0.02^2 = 4 \times 10^{-4}$,
$8 \times 10^{-6}$ and $6.4 \times 10^{-11}$. With $17\,280$ heartbeats a day, $x = 10\,\mathrm{s}$ marks a connected user
offline about seven times a day; Xu's $30\,\mathrm{s}$ almost never does.

## Python

The ranges and the false-offline rates.

```{.python .run}
h, loss = 5, 0.02
for x in (10, 15, 30):
    p = loss ** (x // h)
    print(f"x = {x:2d} s: mark after {x - h}-{x} s; false offline {p:.1e} per heartbeat, {p * 86400 / h:.2g} per day")
```

```{.text .run-output}
x = 10 s: mark after 5-10 s; false offline 4.0e-04 per heartbeat, 6.9 per day
x = 15 s: mark after 10-15 s; false offline 8.0e-06 per heartbeat, 0.14 per day
x = 30 s: mark after 25-30 s; false offline 6.4e-11 per heartbeat, 1.1e-06 per day
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise estimates the herd of @exm-rt-liu-ws-balancer. Clients reconnect at once unless they wait a random time.

::: {#exr-poll-reconnect-herd}
#### The reconnection herd

A connection server with $10^6$ clients fails. Each client reconnects after a delay uniform on $[0, J]$. Give the
reconnection rate for $J = 1$, $10$ and $60\,\mathrm{s}$, and the TLS handshakes per second the other servers must absorb.
If each server can do $2 \times 10^4$ handshakes per second and $33$ servers remain, which $J$ is safe?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The reconnections are spread evenly over $[0, J]$ in expectation, at $10^6/J$ per second: $10^6$, $10^5$ and $1.7 \times
10^4$. Each is a new TLS handshake. The remaining servers absorb $33 \times 2 \times 10^4 = 6.6 \times 10^5$ per second, so
$J \geq 10^6/6.6 \times 10^5 = 1.5\,\mathrm{s}$ suffices on average; a margin for the random fluctuations and for the
servers' normal load suggests $J = 10\,\mathrm{s}$ or more.

## Python

Rates and the smallest safe $J$, with a seeded check of the busiest second for $J = 10$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
clients, capacity = 1e6, 33 * 2e4
for J in (1, 10, 60):
    print(f"J = {J:2d} s: {clients / J:,.0f} reconnections/s")
print(f"smallest J on average: {clients / capacity:.2f} s")
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
t = rng.uniform(0, 10, int(clients))
print(f"busiest second with J = 10: {np.bincount(t.astype(int)).max():,} reconnections")
```

```{.text .run-output}
J =  1 s: 1,000,000 reconnections/s
J = 10 s: 100,000 reconnections/s
J = 60 s: 16,667 reconnections/s
smallest J on average: 1.52 s
busiest second with J = 10: 100,238 reconnections
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise sizes the connection servers for push to every connected user of the photo service. It is the push
design of part (c) at the scale of the running example.

::: {#exr-poll-push-servers}
#### Servers for push

A third of $10^8$ daily users are connected at the peak, a connection server holds $10^6$ connections (as in
@exr-load-chat), and the servers are spread over three zones so that the service survives the loss of one zone. Give the
number of servers, the heartbeat messages per second with $\Delta_{\mathrm{hb}} = 30\,\mathrm{s}$, and the event messages per second if each
user receives $20$ notifications a day, a third of them at the peak hour's rate.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$3.3 \times 10^7$ connections need $34$ servers; to survive the loss of one of three zones each zone needs $\lceil 34/2\rceil =
17$, $51$ in all. Heartbeats: $3.3 \times 10^7/30 = 1.1 \times 10^6$ per second, small frames. Notifications: $2 \times
10^9$ a day, $2.3 \times 10^4$ per second on average; with a peak factor of $3$, $6.9 \times 10^4$ per second. The
heartbeats outnumber the events, as in @exm-poll-heartbeats.

## Python

The three numbers.

```{.python .run}
from math import ceil
connected = 1e8 / 3
servers = ceil(connected / 1e6)
print(f"servers {servers}, with a spare zone {3 * ceil(servers / 2)}")
print(f"heartbeats {connected / 30:,.0f}/s; notifications mean {1e8 * 20 / 86400:,.0f}/s, peak {3 * 1e8 * 20 / 86400:,.0f}/s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
servers 34, with a spare zone 51
heartbeats 1,111,111/s; notifications mean 23,148/s, peak 69,444/s
```
::::
:::
::::

## Authentication and authorisation {#sec-auth}

Every request that reaches the application must answer two questions before it is served. Sinha and Chopra put them
plainly: authentication answers "Who are you?", and authorisation "Are you allowed to do that?"
[@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 8, "API security"]. Liu shows why they cannot be skipped: if `transfer_money(amount,
user_id, to_user_id)` lets "the client ... specify any user_id", anyone can move anyone's money
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "API Security Considerations"]. None of the benchmark books gives the subject a
chapter; Tan's appendix comes closest [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, App. B]. This section fills that gap with two
definitions. The first fixes what a request carries to prove who sent it (a session cookie or a bearer token) and what the
server checks; the second is the OAuth 2.0 authorisation-code grant with OpenID Connect, the standard by which one service
lets a user grant another limited access without sharing a password, and by which a user logs in with an account held
elsewhere. Cryptography itself is outside the tutorial: signatures and keys are used as the standards specify them.

For more on this topic, see @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [App. B and Sec. 13.3], @sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024 [Ch. 8, "API
security"], @liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 5, "Security", and App. 6] and @gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024
[Ch. 10, "Securing the perimeter" to "Securing BFF services"].

### Sessions and tokens

Tan describes the simplest scheme. After the user's password is verified, "the backend creates a session for this user",
the browser receives a cookie with the session's identifier, and "each time the browser makes a request to the backend,
the browser will send the session ID to the backend" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, App. B.2, p. 404]. A token works the
other way round: instead of an identifier that the server looks up, the request carries a statement that the server can
verify by itself. The definition covers both and the checks that go with them.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-auth-session-token}
#### Authentication, authorisation, sessions and tokens

Let a service receive requests on behalf of **principals** (users or other services).

1. **Authentication** is the verification that a request comes from a given principal. **Authorisation** is the decision
   whether that principal may apply the requested operation to the requested resource, by a policy such as role-based
   access control (permissions attached to roles, roles to principals) or attribute-based access control (rules on
   attributes of the principal, the resource and the context).
2. A **credential** is the secret by which a principal first authenticates, such as a password, which the service stores
   only salted and hashed, or an API key. The service then issues a shorter-lived proof that later requests carry instead.
3. A **session** is a record (identifier, principal, expiry) kept by the service in a store; the client presents the
   identifier, usually in a cookie set with `Set-Cookie` and the attributes `Secure` (sent only over TLS), `HttpOnly`
   (hidden from scripts) and `Max-Age` [@rfc6265, Secs. 4.1.2.2, 4.1.2.5 and 4.1.2.6]. Each request is authenticated by
   looking the identifier up; deleting the record **revokes** the session at once.
4. A **bearer token** is a string such that "any party in possession of the token (a 'bearer') can use the token in any
   way that any other party in possession of it can" [@rfc6750, Sec. 1.2], sent in the field `Authorization: Bearer`. An
   **opaque** token is checked by asking its issuer. A **self-contained** token carries its claims and a signature: a
   **JSON Web Token** (JWT) is a header, a set of claims and a signature, each base64url-encoded and joined by periods,
   with claims such as the issuer `iss`, the subject `sub`, the audience `aud` and the expiry `exp`, "on or after which the
   JWT MUST NOT be accepted" [@rfc7519, Secs. 3 and 4.1]. A self-contained token is validated without any lookup, by
   checking its signature, issuer, audience and expiry, and cannot be revoked before it expires without one.
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Sinha and Chopra's two questions separate two checks that every request needs. The status codes of HTTP keep them apart
too.

::: {#exm-auth-two-questions}
#### Two questions, two status codes

A request without valid credentials fails authentication and is answered `401 Unauthorized`, which asks the client to
authenticate; a request from an authenticated user who may not perform the operation fails authorisation and is
answered `403 Forbidden`. Tan's layer-7 balancer "can return 401 if a specified authentication header is absent"
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 3.1.2, p. 57], but only the service that knows the policy can return 403.
:::

Tan's simple login is item 3 of the definition. The cookie carries the session's identifier.

::: {#exm-auth-simple-login}
#### Cookie-based login

After verification, Tan's UI "will set a cookie in the user's browser, such as Set-Cookie: sessionid=f00b4r; Max-Age:
86400;" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, App. B.2, p. 404]. The syntax of the standard is `Max-Age=86400` [@rfc6265,
Sec. 4.1.2.2], and a session cookie should also carry `Secure` and `HttpOnly`: `Set-Cookie: sessionid=f00b4r;
Max-Age=86400; Secure; HttpOnly`. The server stores (`f00b4r`, user, expiry) and looks it up on every request.
:::

Sessions end in two ways. Tan names both.

::: {#exm-auth-timeouts}
#### Absolute and inactivity timeouts

"Absolute timeout terminates the session after a specified period has elapsed. Inactivity timeout terminates the
[session] after a specified period during which a user has not interacted with the application"
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, App. B.2, p. 404]. A banking site might use $15$ minutes of inactivity and $12$ hours absolute;
a photo service $30$ days of inactivity. Each request with a session extends the inactivity deadline, which is a write to
the session store.
:::

Role-based access control attaches permissions to roles. Sinha and Chopra explain why that is simpler.

::: {#exm-auth-rbac}
#### Roles

In role-based access control "permissions are associated with roles, and users are assigned roles", which "simplifies
managing permissions as you only need to manage roles, not individual user permissions"; attribute-based control
"provides more fine-grained control than RBAC but can be more complex to implement" [@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 8,
"Authorization"]. The photo service needs both: a moderator role may hide any photo, and the attribute rule "the
principal is the photo's owner" lets a user delete their own.
:::

Liu's money transfer shows the commonest authorisation bug. The principal must come from the proof of identity, not from
the request's parameters.

::: {#exm-auth-liu-transfer}
#### Whose money?

In `transfer_money(amount, user_id, to_user_id)` the question is "what if the client can specify any user_id ... What kind
of validation should this have?" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "API Security Considerations"]. The source account
must be the authenticated principal (the session's user or the token's `sub`), and the parameter `user_id` should be
removed or checked against it; otherwise authentication succeeds and authorisation is never asked.
:::

A JWT is three encoded parts. RFC 7519's example can be decoded by hand.

::: {#exm-auth-jwt}
#### The parts of a JWT

The example header is `{"typ":"JWT", "alg":"HS256"}`, encoded `eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLA0KICJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9`; the claims are
`{"iss":"joe", "exp":1300819380, "http://example.com/is_root":true}`; and the signature is an HMAC SHA-256 of the first
two encoded parts, `dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk` [@rfc7519, Sec. 3.1]. Anyone can decode the claims; only
a holder of the key can produce a matching signature. The token expired in March 2011, so a server must reject it.
:::

Gilbert's gateway validates tokens before any business logic runs. The checks are those of item 4.

::: {#exm-auth-gilbert-authorizer}
#### Validation at the gateway

"The authorization process verifies the signature of the token and checks the expiration time, at a minimum. The process
will usually validate the issuer and the intended audience as well", and the identity provider publishes its public keys
"following the JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) standard" at a URL that the gateway is configured with
[@gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024, Ch. 10, "JWT authorizer"]. The gateway thus authenticates every request without
a call to the provider.
:::

Bearer tokens must travel encrypted. Gilbert states the reason.

::: {#exm-auth-encryption-in-transit}
#### Why TLS is required

"All calls to a BFF and ESG service must encrypt the data in transit. At a minimum, this is necessary to secure the JWT
bearer token. A bearer token gives access to any bearer of the token, so we must not expose it in transit"
[@gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024, Ch. 10, "Encryption in transit"]. Liu's man-in-the-middle on public Wi-Fi
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Man in the Middle Attack"] would otherwise copy the token and use it, which by the
